rows.hash: ChainHash, 1 KB blocks (W=128, S=2; SMHasher3 name chainhash-1k)
rows.bound: Almost-universal: eps <= (p+2)/2^64 = (S*n+2)/2^64 for two distinct messages of at most n blocks, p = S*n sub-blocks (Theorem thm:ph:collision); for this configuration eps = (2*ceil(l/1024)+2)/2^64 for messages of at most l bytes. Also qualified 5-wise independence: for t <= 5 distinct messages the joint output distribution is within C(t,2)*(p+1)/2^64 of uniform (Theorem thm:ph:kwise). Proved information-theoretically for the IDEAL key of W+9 = 137 independent uniform elements of F = F_2[X]/(X^64+X^4+X^3+X+1); the timed and tested implementation expands a 64-bit seed with splitmix64, a 2^64-member subfamily the theorems do not cover (rem:ph:gaps A1); code-vs-definition equivalence is tested (490,022 checks against a bit-serial reference), not proved (A2). Paper score 62 bits = min_L log2(L/eps(L)), attained at L = 1 (eps = 4/2^64).
rows.key_words: 137 = W+9 (128 block-key words kappa, 3 recurrence keys (u,y,z), 5 finalizer coefficients c_0..c_4, 1 twist word tau; 1,096 random bytes for the ideal key; the implementation derives all of them from one 64-bit seed with splitmix64)

rows.hash: Injective three-key recurrence, one chain, F_{2^64} (Ahle-Knudsen; P_0 = z, P_i = a_i + (b_i + y)(P_{i-1} + u))
rows.bound: eps-almost universal with eps = n/|F| = n/2^64 on messages of 2n field elements (n = number of (a_i,b_i) pairs = ceil(L/2) for L 64-bit words): the difference of two distinct messages' key polynomials is nonzero of total degree <= n (Lemma lem:injective:coeffmap gives injectivity with an explicit decoder), so Schwartz-Zippel over uniform (u,y,z) applies. Proved, information-theoretic, no computational assumption; the paper's bench draws the key uniformly. Paper score 64 bits (min over L, attained at L = 1: n = 1, eps = 2^-64; L = 2n >= 2 gives 65).
rows.smhasher3: Not registered (neither upstream nor on the fork); not in rurban's table.

rows.reference: Ahle and Knudsen 2026, sections/injective.tex lines 6-44 (Definition def:injective:recurrence, bound sentence lines 41-43, Lemma lem:injective:coeffmap); table row "This paper, one chain, $\F_{2^{64}}$ & 3 & 64 & 4.1 & 10.1" (line 323).

rows.hash: Injective three-key recurrence, 8 interleaved lanes, F_{2^64} (fourth key w combines the lanes)
rows.bound: eps <= (ceil(N/L) + L - 1)/2^64 for N pairs dealt to L = 8 lanes: each lane holds at most ceil(N/L) pairs and the lane states are combined as sum_j P_j w^j, so the difference polynomial in (u,y,z,w) is nonzero of total degree <= ceil(N/L)+L-1 (Schwartz-Zippel over four uniform keys). This formula is taken from the harness comment tools/bench/adversarial/speed_hashes.h lines 142-146 (struct PaperGF64Lanes), not from the checked records; the paper table prints 61 bits, which equals min_L log2(L/eps) at L = 1 word (eps = 8/2^64). Proved for uniform keys.
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 60.09 -- formula eps = (ceil(N/8) + 7)/2^64 with N = 64 pairs (128 words): 8+7 = 15, eps = 15/2^64, log2(1/eps) = 64 - log2 15 = 60.09 (formula source: harness comment, see bound)

rows.hash: Injective recurrence, single-key specialization (y = x^3, z = x, u = x^2), F_{2^64}

rows.hash: Injective three-key recurrence over F_{2^89-1} (paper row "This paper, F_{2^89-1} (89-bit output)")
rows.bound: Three-key bound n/p, p = 2^89-1, on 2n field elements (single-key form (3n-1)/p). Paper table: key 5, 88 bits, output the full 89-bit residue (the appendix shows the low 64 bits of an 89-bit Mersenne residue are NOT a safe output: a pair differing by 2^64-1 in the last word collides with probability 2^-25). Caveat (checked): the harness struct that produced the timings, PaperMers89Smart, is a two-key form (x in [0,p), y in [0,2^63)) with 15-byte steps whose own comment bounds Pr[collision] <= (N+2)*2/2^64, and it returns the LOW 64 bits of the residue; the 88-bit score presumes the full residue and field-uniform keys. The paper's 88 is reproduced by min_N log2((15N/8)*2^89/(N+2)) = 88.32 at N = 1 (two-key form with y uniform in F_p); the three-key n/|F| form on 2n words would give 90, not 89.
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 82.85 -- formula eps = (N+2)/p with p = 2^89-1, N = ceil(1024/15) = 69 fifteen-byte steps and y uniform in F_p (the reading that reproduces the table's 88): eps = 71/2^89, log2(1/eps) = 89 - log2 71 = 82.85. Alternatives: three-key n/p with field elements packed 11 bytes each (94 elements, n = 47): 89 - log2 47 = 83.44; the harness comment's own bound (N+2)/2^63 with y drawn from 2^63 values and low-64-bit output: 63 - log2 71 = 56.85
rows.key_words: 5 as printed (harness: x = 2 words, x^2 = 2 words, y = 1 word)
rows.output_bits: 89 as printed in the table (full residue); the timed harness code returns the low 64 bits

rows.hash: PolymurHash 2.0 (Orson R. L. Peters, 2023)
rows.bound: Almost-universal: for two distinct inputs of at most n bytes, Pr[collision] <= (14 + n/7)/|K| with |K| = totient(2^61-2)*(2^60-2^56)/(2^61-1), log2|K| = 57.4028 (k restricted to generators of the multiplicative group mod 2^61-1 with k^7 < 2^60-2^56); stated by the author after dropping the +14 as n/7 * 2^-57.4 = n * 2^-60.2. Almost pairwise independent: Pr[H(m)=x and H(m')=y] <= n * 2^-124.2, which needs s uniform on 2^64 (128 bits of entropy). Proof is the informal extras/universality-proof.md (no formal verification; bounds-check.py simulation only). Assumes k uniform on K and independent of the inputs: polymur_init_params derives k deterministically from k_seed by a rejection walk, so the induced distribution is only approximately uniform; polymur_init_params_from_seed gives a 2^64-member subfamily; no claim is made for hashes with different tweaks. Paper score 57 bits (per word: 8L * 2^-60.2 = L * 2^-57.2).
rows.key_words: 4 resident (struct PolymurHashParams {k, k2, k7, s} = 32 bytes); secret input 2 x 64-bit words (k_seed, s_seed) or one 64-bit seed; effective entropy ~57.4 bits for k plus 64 bits for s
rows.smhasher3: Registered upstream (family polymur, src_status SRC_STABLEISH, FLAG_HASH_XL_SEED; hashes/polymur.cpp is a re-implementation ported from commit a7cc6b0 = v2.0 HEAD). polymurhash (params re-derived from each seed): 250/250 passed, verification LE 0x0722B1A7. polymurhash-tweakseed (params fixed from seed 0, SMHasher seed used as tweak): 243/250, 7 failures all SeedBIC : [3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 15, 52] (the 28- and 1024-byte SeedBIC rows passed). Results from SMHasher3 20251015-release-5035a923 (raw files last regenerated in commit ea0b94f9, 2025-10-16; attribution inferred). rurban/smhasher (submodule pinned at v1.0): polymur 41.68 cycles/hash, no quality problems listed. Author's fork SeedDifferential extended tier: 0 collisions in 2^30 seeds for both variants.

rows.speed_m2_gbps: 19.7 (16 KB) / 16.2 (512 B); row "Polymur (random k, s)" in adversarial_table/speed_new.txt (19.6602 / 16.1894, 9 runs), polymur_init_params with two random words, tweak 0. Author-reported: Apple M1 33.3 GiB/s (11.6 bytes/cycle), <= 49 bytes in 21 cycles.
rows.reference: Orson R. L. Peters, PolymurHash (GitHub repository description "The PolymurHash universal hash function."), version 2.0, 2023, https://github.com/orlp/polymur-hash; proof: extras/universality-proof.md; README lines 7-14. No paper. The title "PolymurHash: a universal hash function with a proven collision bound" is the wording of the paper's references.bib entry (key polymur), not the author's. Last commit a7cc6b00 (2023-06-23, "Add ULL suffix to reference values."); v2.0 commit c6cc6884 "Changed behavior for the empty string, now depends on seed for MinHash/HyperLogLog-esque algorithms." zlib license; C header-only; no SIMD (needs 64x64->128 multiply).

rows.hash: UMASH-64 (Paul Khuong / Backtrace I/O; umash_full, which == 0)
rows.bound: Almost-universal: for any two inputs of s bytes or fewer, Pr[same 64-bit hash] < ceil(s/4096) * 2^-55 (README and 2022 whitepaper; in 64-bit words eps < ceil(L/512) * 2^-55). Derived by case analysis as a composition of 2^-64-almost-xor-universal PH, 2^-64-almost-universal ENH and a Carter-Wegman polynomial over Z/(2^61-1), with the constants hand-rounded ("let's conservatively bump that to $\varepsilon < 2^{-55}$"); the README calls it "a proof sketch for the collision bound"; not peer-reviewed. Assumes a uniformly random, input-independent full key; the 64-bit "seed" is only a hint; umash_params_derive expands a 64-bit value + 32-byte secret with Salsa20, a pseudo-random subfamily. Linear: collisions combine. The 2020 blog's ceil(s/2048) * 2^-56 is superseded. Paper score 55 bits.
rows.key_words: 38 (struct umash_params: poly[2][2] = 4 words + oh[32 + 2] = 34 words = 304 bytes; the which==0 64-bit hash reads 34 of them; the paper charges 38)
rows.smhasher3: Registered upstream (hashes/umash.cpp, family src_status SRC_ACTIVE, compiled only under HAVE_X86_64_CLMUL, impl hwclmul). "Failing hashes" table: UMASH-64: 123/250 passed, 127 tests failed, exactly 90 of them Seed* tests (the 64-bit seed is 'merely a hint'); UMASH-64.reseed (full key re-derived per seed via Salsa20): 214/250 passed, 36 failed: BIC [3, 4, 6, 8]; Zeroes []; Sparse [9/4, 6/8, 3/96, 2/512, 2/1024, 2/1280, 2/1536, 2/2048]; Permutation (all 20); Bitflip [4]; SeedZeroes [1280, 8448] (91 failures disappear under reseeding: 88 Seed* plus PerlinNoise [2, 4, 8]; SeedZeroes persists). Results from SMHasher3 20251015-release-5035a923 (raw files from commit ea0b94f9). rurban/smhasher (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G): umash64 26628.37 MiB/sec, 39.87 cycl./hash, no quality problems; README lists "umash (even universal!)" among the fastest without quality problems (32-bit halves claim carries the caveat "after expanding each seed to a 320-byte key" for demerphq's suite).

rows.reference: Paul Khuong, "UMASH: a fast almost universal 64-bit string hash", Backtrace I/O whitepaper dated 2022-02-23 (umash.pdf rendered from umash_reference.py, https://github.com/backtrace-labs/umash/blob/master/umash.pdf); announced as "UMASH: a fast and universal enough hash", Backtrace Engineering blog, 2020-08-24 (https://engineering.backtrace.io/2020-08-24-umash-fast-enough-almost-universal-fingerprinting/); fingerprint revision "Nearly double the PH bits with one more CLMUL", pvk.ca, 2020-10-31. Code https://github.com/backtrace-labs/umash (C, MIT; x86-64 CLMUL or aarch64 crypto/PMULL; algorithm finalized, last push 2026-01-11). No arXiv or peer-reviewed venue. Paper bib @misc{umash} (references.bib lines 434-441, incl. url field).

rows.hash: UMASH-128 fingerprint (umash_fprint = two 64-bit UMASH values computed concurrently)
rows.bound: Almost-universal: two inputs of s bytes or fewer collide on the 128-bit fingerprint with probability < ceil(s/2^26)^2 * 2^-83 (= 2^-83 up to 64 MiB; README: less than 2**-70 for up to 5 GiB; whitepaper: 'less than $2^{-70}$ at 5 GB'; both hold, bound < 2^-70 up to about 6.0 GB). Same proof-sketch status and uniform-full-key assumption as UMASH-64 ("Let's conservatively bump that to $\varepsilon_{fp} < 2^{-83}$"). Paper score 83 bits.

rows.hash: CLHASH (Lemire and Kaser 2016; full variable-length hash, 64-bit)
rows.bound: Almost-XOR-universal (Lemma 9): eps = 2^-64 (XOR-universal) when |s| != |s'| (length term k''|M|) or when both inputs are at most 1024 bytes; for equal lengths above 1 KB eps <= 2/2^64 + (n-1)/2^126 with n = ceil(|M|/1024) 128-word blocks (block-level CLNH 1/2^64 + polynomial over GF(2^127) (n-1)/2^126 + final CLNH reduction 1/2^64), capped by the paper at 2.004/2^64 for all strings up to 2^64 bytes. Proved information-theoretically for Algorithm 4's ideal key (128 uniform 64-bit words, a 126-bit polynomial key, a 128-bit key, a 64-bit key). Not covered: the reference code and SMHasher3 expand a 64- or 128-bit seed with xorshift128plus (the paper used MT19937); the code masks the polynomial key to 126 bits (degree <= 125) and re-draws only the pair (0,1). The BITMIX build applies fmix64 (a bijection, bound unchanged) only on inputs of at most 1024 bytes. Paper metric would give 64 bits (min at L = 1).
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 64.00 -- Lemma 9 / Table 4: inputs of 1-1024 bytes are XOR universal, eps = 2^-64, log2(1/eps) = 64.00 (a 1025-byte equal-length pair would give eps <= 2/2^64 + 1/2^126, 63.00 bits)
rows.key_words: 133 (1064 bytes: 128 CLNH words + 2 for the 126-bit polynomial key + 2 for the 128-bit k' + 1 for k''; clhash.h RANDOM_64BITWORDS_NEEDED_FOR_CLHASH = 133; paper accounting 8510 random bits); seeded from two 64-bit seeds
rows.smhasher3: Registered upstream (hashes/clhash.cpp, family clhash, SRC_STABLEISH, FLAG_HASH_CLMUL_BASED | FLAG_HASH_LOOKUP_TABLE | FLAG_HASH_NO_SEED, x86-64 PCLMUL builds only, key derived as get_random_key_for_clhash(s64, ~s64) from the 64-bit seed). CLhash (without -DBITMIX): 64/250 passed, 186 failed (Avalanche, BIC, Cyclic, Sparse, Permutation, Text, TwoBytes, PerlinNoise, Bitflip, Seed*); CLhash.bitmix: 227/250 passed, 23 failed: BIC [3, 4, 6, 8]; Sparse [5/12, 2/1280, 2/1536, 2/2048]; Permutation [4 64-byte sets]; Text [Long alnum 1968-2128, 4016-4176, 8112-8272]; TwoBytes [2048, 4096]; SeedZeroes [1280, 8448]. Checked interpretation: every failure on inputs longer than 1 KB is in SMHasher3's '---Analyzing differential distribution' pass (four-input relation h(a)^h(b) = h(c)^h(d), which no AXU bound constrains; first-pass 64-bit collisions are 'Expected 0.0, actual 0' on all of those keysets); the ONLY first-pass 64-bit collision failure in either log is Sparse 5/12 ("12-byte keys with up to 5 bits set - 64593561 keys", "Expected 0.0, actual 2"), an open implementation/seeding question. Results from SMHasher3 20251015-release-5035a923 (raw logs from commit ea0b94f9, byte-identical to upstream). rurban/smhasher (BITMIX build, header `carry-less mult. hash -DBITMIX (64-bit for x64, SSE4.2)`): clhash 22932.36 MiB/sec, 67.22 cycl./hash, 262.78 (2) cycl./map, size 1167, quality problems "PerlinNoise, machine-specific (x64 SSE4.2)" (rurban's PerlinNoise varies the seed; the hash is registered NO_SEED in SMHasher3).
rows.speed_smhasher3: CLhash: Avg. cycles (1-32 bytes) 48.19; bulk 7.36 bytes/cycle. CLhash.bitmix: 60.80 cycles; 7.33 bytes/cycle. x86 PCLMUL build.
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Not timed as the full CLHASH in the paper; see the CLNH row (27.3 / 26.3). Author-reported: "On a recent Intel processor (e.g., Skylake), it can hash input strings at a speed of 0.1 cycles per byte for sufficiently long strings. ..."
rows.reference: Daniel Lemire and Owen Kaser, "Faster 64-bit universal hashing using carry-less multiplications", Journal of Cryptographic Engineering 6(3):171-185, Springer, 2016, DOI 10.1007/s13389-015-0110-5; arXiv:1503.03465 (v8, 4 Nov 2015), Section 5, Lemma 9, Table 4 (PDF p. 10), Lemma 5 (Sec. 4.2), Algorithm 4. Code https://github.com/lemire/clhash (C99 + C++ wrapper, Apache-2.0, x64 PCLMULQDQ+SSE4.2 or AArch64 PMULL, active: last commit c35030af 2026-05-23). Paper bib key lemire2015clhash.

rows.hash: CLNH (Lemire-Kaser CLHASH inner hash, fixed length; paper row "CLNH (fixed length)")
rows.bound: XOR-universal (Delta-universal in the binary field) with eps = 2^-64 on same-length inputs: Lemma 5, the family (a1+x1)(a2+x2) + (a3+x3)(a4+x4) + ... over GF(p^n) with all keys uniform, collision probability <= 1/p^n; here carry-less products mod the irreducible 2^64+27. Proved; key must be one uniform 64-bit word per message word. Fixed length only (no length term in this row). Paper score 64 bits.
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 64.00 -- formula eps = 2^-64 at every fixed length (key of L = 128 words for a 1 KB message), log2(1/eps) = 64.00
rows.key_words: L (one 64-bit word per message word; 128 words for 1 KB; the table prints "L")
rows.output_bits: 64 (framework clnh_64: lower 64 bits of the GF(2^64) products, XOR of N products (m_{2i}^x)(m_{2i+1}^x))
rows.smhasher3: Not registered as a separate hash (only the full CLHASH is).
rows.speed_m2_gbps: 27.3 (16 KB) / 26.3 (512 B); framework class clnh_64<N> (tools/bench/framework/injective_hashing_arm.h), adversarial_table/speed_rerun.txt 27.2919 / 26.2514 (RUNS=9 medians on an L1-resident buffer), Apple M2 Pro; described in the paper as "the throughput ceiling of an $O(N)$-key inner product"
rows.reference: Lemire and Kaser 2016, Lemma 5 (Section 4.2) and eq. (7); Ahle and Knudsen 2026, sections/injective.tex table row "CLNH (fixed length)~\cite{lemire2015clhash} & $L$ & 64 & 27.3 & 26.3" (line 344); related.tex: "We include CLHASH (denoted CLNH) in our experimental comparisons as a throughput baseline."

rows.hash: HalftimeHash24 (Jim Apple 2021; paper variant with k = 3, 192-bit output)
rows.bound: eps-almost universal on EQUAL-length strings: eps = 2^{-32k} (2^{kp} + h^k + 1), k = 3 output words = erasure-code minimum distance, p = 2 (the paper writes "p = 2^2" but only p = 2 in the exponent reproduces the stated "more than 83 bits"), h = tree height = floor(log_f floor(n/(b d w))) with (b, d, e, f, k, p, w) = (8, 7, 9, 8, 3, 2^2, 3); the shipped code's GetEntropyBytesNeeded computes h with n in BYTES and the paper's own "8.4KB for one megabyte" reproduces only under that convention (h = 4 at 1 MB, h = 17 at 1 EB; 83.72 bits at h = 17). Proved for uniformly random, independently chosen input entropy (NH 2^-32-ADU from UMAC, Nandi's EHC, the paper's generalized-EHC lemma over Z_{2^64}, Carter-Wegman tree and composition lemmas); different lengths handled by appending the length (asserted, not proved). The paper's "34KB entropy for one exabyte" is not reproduced by its own formula (30.5 KB). No shipped API exposes this variant.
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 89.98 -- formula eps = 2^-96 (2^6 + h^3 + 1) with h = floor(log_8 floor(1024/(8*7*3 = 168))) = floor(log_8 6) = 0 (same with n = 256 32-bit words): eps = 65 * 2^-96, log2(1/eps) = 96 - log2 65 = 89.98. Caveat: applied literally below the hash's design regime (the header says "designed for long strings (> 1KB)"); at 1 MB (h = 4) the formula gives 96 - log2(64 + 64 + 1) = 88.99
rows.key_words: e*w + (f-1)*h*k + b*f*h*k + b*d*w + k - 1 words (paper l.506-511); "HalftimeHash24 requires 8.4KB input entropy for strings of length up to one megabyte" (= 8392 bytes with h = 4; the exabyte figure is inconsistent, see bound); for h = 0 at 1 KB: 27 + 0 + 0 + 168 + 2 = 197 words
rows.output_bits: 192 (k = 3 words of 64 bits); the paper's variants are 128/192/256/320 bits for k = 2..5
rows.smhasher3: Not registered (no API exposes the 192-bit variant); see the shipped 64-bit row.
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Not measured on the M2 Pro (speed_results.json: "vendor/halftime_hash was not benchmarked (not requested)."). Author-reported (abstract, l.41): "exceeding 16 bytes per cycle" (Intel i7-7800X AVX-512); Figure caption: 256KiB strings; l.62: on strings longer than 1KB typically 55% faster than clhash.
rows.reference: Jim Apple, "HalftimeHash: Modern Hashing without 64-bit Multipliers or Finite Fields", arXiv:2104.08865 (submitted 18 Apr 2021), https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08865; Algorithms and Data Structures (WADS 2021), LNCS 12808, Springer, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-83508-8_8. TeX source https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jbapple/HalftimeHash/main/halftime-hash.tex (Section "Cumulative Analysis", l.500-512).

rows.hash: HalftimeHash, shipped 64-bit API (HalftimeHashStyle512/256/128/64; SMHasher3 HalftimeHash-64/128/256/512)
rows.bound: Derived, NOT stated in the paper: the shipped functions run the k = 2 (16-byte) core (p = 2, (d, w) = (6, 3)) and fold to 64 bits by XOR of byte-indexed random tables over the two output words and the length (TabulateAfter<V<2>,2>); composing the k = 2 AU bound with the 2^-64-universal simple-tabulation fold by the Carter-Wegman lemma gives eps ~ 2^-64 (2^4 + h^2 + 2): about 2^-58.9 at 1 MB (h = 4) and 2^-55.7 at 1 EB (h = 17) (derivation by the record author and in tools/bench/adversarial/vendor/halftime_hash/PROVENANCE.txt). Assumes the 70928-byte entropy table is uniformly random; SMHasher3 expands a 64-bit seed with splitmix/romu and upstream's example uses std::mt19937_64 (subfamilies outside the proof). The Style number is the SIMD block width, not the output width; the four styles are different functions.
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 59.83 -- derived formula eps = 2^-64 (2^4 + h^2 + 2) with h = floor(log_8 floor(1024/(8*6*3 = 144))) = floor(log_8 7) = 0: eps = 18 * 2^-64, log2(1/eps) = 64 - log2 18 = 59.83 (not a published bound; applied below the > 1KB design regime)
rows.key_words: 8866 64-bit words (kEntropyBytesNeeded = 70928 bytes: 6144 words of tabulation tables + 2722 words for the k = 2 core sized for unbounded length), compiled from the upstream header (commit caf7924)
rows.smhasher3: Registered upstream (hashes/halftimehash.cpp, SMHasher3 port by Frank J. T. Wojcik 2021-2022, SRC_STABLEISH, MIT notice "Copyright (c) 2020 Jim Apple"), impl tag [avx2]; all four in "Failing hashes": HalftimeHash-64 214/250 (36 failed: Zeroes, Sparse, Permutation, TwoBytes, SeedZeroes); HalftimeHash-128 202/250 (48 failed, + Bitflip); HalftimeHash-256 200/250 (50 failed); HalftimeHash-512 190/250 (60 failed, + Bitflip). Every one of the 231/316/326/403 '!!!!!' lines lies under '---Analyzing differential distribution' (a linearity detector); the direct hash-value collision rows pass in every keyset. Results from SMHasher3 20251015-release-5035a923 (raw files from commit ea0b94f9). The paper's "HalftimeHash passes all correctness and randomness tests in the SMHasher test suite" (l.524) refers to rurban's 2021 suite: rurban rows halftime_hash64 4801.79 MiB/s, 99.05 cycl./hash, no problems; halftime_hash128 18220.34, 94.31, "UB overflow"; halftime_hash256 18249.32, 97.56, "UB overflow"; halftime_hash512 10906.18, 118.54, none. Author's fork seeded-differential sweep (default tier 2^24, portable impl): PASS for all four.
rows.speed_smhasher3: README (Avg. cycles 1-32 bytes; Avg. bytes/cycle bulk = the 'Alignment rnd' line of the [262017, 262144]-byte test): -64: 83.75 cycles, 2.02 B/cycle; -128: 95.58, 6.87; -256: 100.89, 11.70; -512: 113.77, 9.51 (raw 262144-byte 'Average' lines: 2.02 / 6.92 / 11.91 / 9.63). x86 avx2 build.
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Not measured on the M2 Pro (deliberately skipped; the vendored NEON-fixed copy in tools/bench/adversarial/vendor/halftime_hash/ is ready). Upstream header does not compile on AArch64 without the macro-alias fix (arm_neon_fix.h).
rows.reference: Jim Apple, arXiv:2104.08865 / WADS 2021 LNCS 12808 (as above); code https://github.com/jbapple/HalftimeHash (C++17 header-only halftime-hash.hpp, repository LICENSE Apache-2.0, the header itself carries no license notice; last commit on main caf7924 2022-05-28; the 2025-03-08 push is the orphan `supercop` branch c7396eb "Add halftimehash56"; 11 stars).

rows.hash: Poly1305 (D. J. Bernstein 2005; hash H_r(m) = (m(r) mod 2^130-5) mod 2^128)
rows.bound: Delta-universal (differential w.r.t. addition mod 2^128): for distinct messages of at most L bytes and any 16-byte g, Pr_r[H_r(m) = H_r(m') + g] <= 8*ceil(L/16)/2^106 with r uniform over the 2^106-element clamped key set R (Theorem 3.3; proof is a root count of the nonzero polynomial m' - m - u of degree <= ceil(L/16) over Z/(2^130-5), summed over the <= 8 lifts u of g: U is the set of integers in [-2^130+6, 2^130-6] congruent to g mod 2^128, an interval of width 2^131-12 < 8*2^128). Unconditional, information-theoretic, no message-distribution assumption; r may be reused across messages (RFC 8439: r MAY be constant). MAC-level (Poly1305-AES / ChaCha20-Poly1305) additionally assumes AES/ChaCha PRF security (delta), unique nonces / one-time (r,s) pads. In words: eps(L_w) = 8*ceil(L_w/2)/2^106; paper metric 103 bits at L_w = 1 (104 for even L_w).
rows.key_words: 2 (r is one 128-bit value with 22 clamped bits, 106 bits of entropy: "r[3], r[7], r[11], r[15] are required to have their top four bits clear ... r[4], r[8], r[12] are required to have their bottom two bits clear ... Thus there are 2^106 possibilities for r"); the MAC adds a 128-bit one-time pad s (AES_k(n) or half of the RFC 8439 32-byte one-time key) = 4 words per MAC key; implementations keep r plus ~2-4 precomputed words
rows.output_bits: 128 ("the 16-byte unsigned little-endian representation of (m(r) mod 2^130 - 5) mod 2^128"; internal residue 130 bits, truncation costs the factor 8)
rows.smhasher3: Not registered (no poly1305 row, raw file or source in upstream results through 20260827-release-22-c378d845 or in any local clone); not in rurban's table.
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Not in the paper's table. Indicative local measurements on an Apple M2 Pro (2026-09-17, machine not idle, +-15%): OpenSSL 3.6.4 EVP_MAC POLY1305 per message (init+update+final, NEON poly1305-armv8): 2.09-2.38 GB/s at 512 B, 3.23-3.25 GB/s at 16 KB; poly1305-donna 64-bit (__int128, clang -O3, full poly1305_auth per message): 0.94-1.30 GB/s at 512 B, 1.08-1.15 GB/s at 16 KB. OpenSSL's own tables: Apple A7 NEON 0.72 cycles/byte; Skylake AVX-512 0.35 c/B.
rows.reference: Daniel J. Bernstein, "The Poly1305-AES message-authentication code", pages 32-49 in Fast software encryption: 12th international workshop, FSE 2005, Paris, France, February 21-23, 2005, revised selected papers (edited by Henri Gilbert, Helena Handschuh), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 3557, Springer, 2005, ISBN 3-540-26541-4; document ID 0018d9551b5546d97c340e0dd8cb5750, dated 2005.03.29, https://cr.yp.to/mac/poly1305-20050329.pdf (Section 3, Theorem 3.3, PDF p. 8; "Keys" subsection of Section 2, p. 4). Standardized in Y. Nir, A. Langley, RFC 8439 (June 2018). Implementations: poly1305-donna (https://github.com/floodyberry/poly1305-donna, public domain, last commit e6ad6e0 2016-03-29 UTC); OpenSSL crypto/poly1305/ (portable C; x86_64 perlasm with integer, AVX, AVX2 and AVX-512F paths; armv8 integer and NEON); BoringSSL crypto/poly1305/ (poly1305.cc portable, poly1305_vec.cc SSE2 x86_64, poly1305_arm.cc 32-bit ARM NEON).

rows.hash: GHASH (McGrew-Viega 2004; GCM's polynomial hash over GF(2^128))
rows.bound: Almost-XOR-universal (Lemma 2, eprint 2004/193 Appendix A): GHASH is ceil(l/w + 1) * 2^-t-almost xor universal when the AAD and ciphertext lengths sum to at most l bits, block width w = 128, output truncated to t bits; at full width eps = (p+1)/2^128 with p the number of 128-bit blocks (the +1 is the appended length block); proof: the polynomial R(H) has at most p+1 roots, H uniform in GF(2^128). Unconditional for uniform H and the designers' length-appending GHASH(H, A, C); in GCM H = E_K(0^128) is only pseudorandom, so the deployed bound adds the block-cipher PRP/PRF advantage. NIST's simplified GHASH_H (no length block) "does not obtain all of the properties that are shown for the designers' definition" and is approved only inside GCM; truncating the tag to t bits scales eps by 2^(128-t) (NIST: targeted forgery ~ n/2^t). The 2012 Iwata-Ohashi-Minematsu repair concerns GCM's counter-collision lemma (non-96-bit IVs), not Lemma 2. H = 0 (prob. 2^-128) makes GHASH constant. Paper metric: 127 bits at L_w = 1, tending to 129.
rows.key_words: 2 (hash subkey H is one 128-bit field element; in GCM derived as E_K(0^128) from the AES key); fast implementations keep H..H^4 or H..H^8 plus Karatsuba pre-sums resident: OpenSSL ghashv8-armx fills 12 of a declared 16 x 128-bit Htable (24 of 32 words), ghash-x86_64 CLMUL 6 x 128-bit (12 words); 4-bit table code 256 B or 528 B per key
rows.output_bits: 128 (one GF(2^128) block; GCM tags may be truncated to t = 96..128, or 32/64 under SP 800-38D Appendix C restrictions)
rows.smhasher3: Not registered (no ghash/gcm row or source upstream or in any local clone); not in rurban's table.
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Not in the paper's table. Indicative local measurements on an Apple M2 Pro: `openssl speed ghash` (OpenSSL 3.6.4, streamed GHASH via ghashv8-armx PMULL, no per-message setup): 6.44-6.48 GB/s at 512 B and 6.92-6.98 GB/s at 16 KB (size assignment by run order; the +F lines carry no size label); a re-run with explicit -bytes gave 6.97 GB/s at 512 B and 7.33 GB/s at 16 KB; EVP_MAC GMAC/AES-128-GCM per message (includes AES key schedule + H derivation): 0.43-0.45 GB/s at 512 B, 2.68-3.12 GB/s at 16 KB. OpenSSL's own table: Apple A7 PMULL 0.58 cycles/byte.
rows.reference: David A. McGrew and John Viega, "The Security and Performance of the Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) of Operation", Progress in Cryptology - INDOCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3348, Springer, pp. 343-355, DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-30556-9_27; full version Cryptology ePrint Archive 2004/193, https://eprint.iacr.org/2004/193.pdf (Appendix A, Lemma 2). Morris Dworkin, NIST SP 800-38D (Nov 2007), DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-38D (Sec. 6.4 Algorithm 2, footnote 1 p. 9, Appendix B). Correction: Iwata, Ohashi, Minematsu, "Breaking and Repairing GCM Security Proofs", CRYPTO 2012, https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/438. Implementations: OpenSSL crypto/modes/asm/ghash-x86_64.pl (PCLMULQDQ) and ghashv8-armx.pl (PMULL); BoringSSL aesv8-gcm-armv8.pl, aesni-gcm-x86_64.pl, aes-gcm-avx2/avx512-x86_64.pl.

rows.hash: NH[n,w] (UMAC inner hash; Black, Halevi, Krawczyk, Krovetz, Rogaway 1999)
rows.bound: 2^-w-almost universal (and 2^-w-A-Delta-U under addition mod 2^{2w}) on distinct EQUAL-length strings of 2w..nw bits, n even (Theorem 4.2); the bound is tight (M = 0^w 0^w vs 1^w 0^w collide whenever K2 = 0^w). Signed NHS[n,w]: 2^{-w+1}-AU (Theorem 4.5); Toeplitz NHT[n,w,t]: 2^{-wt}-AU with key w(n + 2(t-1)) bits (Theorem 5.1). Proved, information-theoretic, for a uniformly random nw-bit key K; replacing either addition with XOR breaks the bound. Equal-length restriction (removed at the UHASH/VHASH level by length encoding and the polynomial layer); the 2007 eprint notes NH is (2^-w)-ADU over messages that are any multiple of 2w bits (but no longer than nw bits).
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 64.00 for w = 64 -- formula eps = 2^-w on equal-length inputs of at most nw bits, which at 1 KB requires n >= 128 64-bit words (key 128 words = 1 KB); log2(1/eps) = 64.00. With w = 32 (UMAC's word size) eps = 2^-32 per 32-bit output stream, 32.00 bits (NHS: 31.00)
rows.key_words: nw/64 words = one key word per message word: NH[16,64] (VHASH L1) = 16 words = 128 B; RFC 4418 UHASH L1Key = 1024 bytes = 128 words (unsigned NH on 1024-byte chunks); the 1999 paper's UMAC-STD NH[1024,32] = 1024 32-bit words = 4096 B = 512 words; 128 words for a 1 KB message at w = 64
rows.smhasher3: Not registered as a stand-alone hash (only VHASH is); not in rurban's table.
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Not in the paper's table (the paper composes its recurrence with "the reduction-free inner level of the NH-based hybrids, in the same way that UMAC, VMAC and CLHASH compose a polynomial with NH"). Closest measured relative: CLNH 27.3 / 26.3.
rows.reference: J. Black, S. Halevi, H. Krawczyk, T. Krovetz, P. Rogaway, "UMAC: Fast and Secure Message Authentication", Advances in Cryptology - CRYPTO '99, LNCS 1666, Springer, 1999, pp. 216-233, DOI 10.1007/3-540-48405-1_14; full version dated August 4, 1999, https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/papers/umac-full.pdf (Section 4.3 Theorem 4.2, Section 4.4 Theorem 4.5, Section 5.2 Theorem 5.1). Paper bib key black1999umac.

rows.hash: UMAC / UHASH (RFC 4418, March 2006; UMAC-32/64/96/128)
rows.bound: Wegman-Carter MAC over UHASH (L1 = unsigned NH mod 2^64 on 32-bit words per 1024-byte chunk, L2 = polynomial mod 2^64-59 / 2^128-159, L3 = inner product mod 2^36-5 -> 32 bits per iteration). RFC 4418: with truly random keys and pads, forgery probability per attempt is no more than 1/2^30, 1/2^60, 1/2^90, 1/2^120 for 32/64/96/128-bit tags (N/2^60 over N attempts), messages < 2^67 bits, at most 2^64 messages per key; UHASH's collision property "is proven unconditionally". As deployed all internal keys and pads are derived from a 16-byte AES key (KDF/PDF), adding 3*delta_AES (computational). Nonce must never repeat. The hash-level collision bound of the standardized UHASH is not restated in the RFC; the 1999 paper's UMAC-STD used the signed NHS (2^-31 per stream), "helps explain the 2^-30 and 2^-60 forging probabilities".
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 60.00 for UMAC-64 -- the RFC's forgery bound 1/2^60 is length-independent for messages below 2^67 bits; log2(1/eps) = 60.00 (UMAC-32: 30.00; UMAC-96: 90.00; UMAC-128: 120.00), plus 3*delta_AES
rows.key_words: UMAC-64 internal key 1224 B = 153 words (RFC 4418 5.1: L1Key 1024 + (iters-1)*16 bytes, L2Key iters*24, L3Key1 iters*64, L3Key2 iters*4; UMAC-32 1116 B, UMAC-128 1440 B = 180 words); external key 16 B (AES-128)
rows.smhasher3: Not registered; not in rurban's table.
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Not in the paper's table. Authors' figures: 0.98 cycles/byte (2^-60) / 0.51 cpb (2^-30) on a 350 MHz Pentium II (CRYPTO '99).
rows.reference: T. Krovetz (ed.), "UMAC: Message Authentication Code using Universal Hashing", RFC 4418, March 2006, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4418.txt (Sections 1, 6.1, 6.2); Black et al. CRYPTO '99 (as above). Reference code https://fastcrypto.org/umac/2004/code.html (umac.c "Version 0.92 of draft-krovetz-umac-07.txt -- 2006 February 21", not maintained upstream; OpenSSH carries its own umac.c "Version 0.93b of rfc4418.txt -- 2006 July 18").

rows.hash: VHASH-64 / VMAC (Krovetz 2006; Dai-Krovetz 2007 revision as specified in draft-krovetz-vmac-01)
rows.bound: Almost-Delta-universal. Theorem 1 (eprint 2007/338): VHASH[b] is eps-ADU for addition modulo p = 2^64-257 over all binary strings up to l bits (l a multiple of b, b = L1 key bits = 1024) with eps = 1/2^62 + 1/(2^64-257) + (l/b)*2^-115; Corollary 2 (addition mod 2^64): eps = 1/2^61 + 2/(2^64-257) + (l/b)*2^-114. Fig. 1: (2^-61)-ADU for all messages up to 2^62 bits when K, k, k1, k2 are chosen randomly and b = 1024 (this headline holds for Theorem 1: at l = 2^62 the total is 0.875 * 2^-61; the mod-2^64 corollary gives 1.75 * 2^-61). The SAC 2006 original (L3 mod 2^61-1) had eps = 2^-59.9 + (l/b)*2^-107. VMAC forgery: < 1/2^60 (64-bit tag) or 1/2^120 (128-bit) with truly random keys and pads, plus delta_AES as deployed (keys from a 16-byte AES key via KDF). Proved for K, k, k1, k2 uniform; VHASH-128 = two iterations with shifted keys.
rows.key_words: VHASH-64: 20 words = 160 B (L1 key 1024 bits = 16 words, L2 key 128 bits = 2 words, L3 key 2 x 64 bits = 2 words; "VMAC uses 160 bytes"; SMHasher3 vmac.cpp nhkey[16] + polykey[2] + l3key[2]); VHASH-128: 26 words = 208 B; external key 16 B (AES)
rows.output_bits: 64 per iteration (range Z_{2^64-257}); VHASH-64 = 64, VHASH-128 = 128; SMHasher3 VHASH = 64, VHASH.32 = low 32 bits
rows.smhasher3: Registered upstream (family vmac, src_url https://www.fastcrypto.org/vmac/, SRC_FROZEN, portable impl, FLAG_HASH_CRYPTOGRAPHIC). VHASH (64-bit): 190/250 passed; failing: Avalanche [3]; BIC [3]; Zeroes []; Sparse [6/2, 10/2]; Permutation [12 sets]; TwoBytes [20, 48]; PerlinNoise [2, 4, 8]; Bitflip [3]; SeedZeroes [1280, 8448]; SeedSparse [2, 3, 6, 15, 18, 31, 52, 80]; SeedBlockOffset [0..9]; Seed [2, 3, 6, 15, 18, 31, 52, 80]; SeedAvalanche [3, 4]; SeedBIC [3, 4]; SeedBitflip [3, 4, 8, 20, 32]. VHASH.32: 194/250 (same list without SeedAvalanche/SeedBIC). Caveat: the wrapper uses the fixed key "abcdefghijklmnop" and "Homegrown (unofficial) seeding" (seed XORed into the poly key), so the Seed* failures test a non-standard interface. Results consistent with SMHasher3 20251015-release-5035a923 (raw files from commit ea0b94f9; inferred). rurban/smhasher: "| [VHASH_64](doc/VHASH_64.txt) | 13217.64 | 64.90 | 270.04 (2) |1231 | sanity, Seed, Sparse |" and "| [VHASH_32](doc/VHASH_32.txt) | 13084.37 | 65.45 | 280.14 (2) |1231 | sanity, Seed, MomentChi2 |".

rows.hash: Vector / pair multiply-shift (Dietzfelbinger 1996; Thorup's notes eqs. (17), (18), (20); paper row "Multiply-shift (fixed length)")
rows.bound: Strongly universal (exactly 2-independent): for w-bit words, l-bit output, wbar >= w + l - 1 and d+1 independent uniform keys a_0..a_{d-1}, b in [2^wbar], any distinct fixed-length vectors x != y in [2^w]^d satisfy Pr[h(x) = q and h(y) = r] = 2^-2l for all q, r, hence eps = Pr[h(x) = h(y)] = 2^-l exactly, independent of d (Theorem 3.7; "collision probability 1/2^l"). Pair-multiply-shift (18) halves the multiplications (Exercise 3.10); the prefix form (20) with a length-indexed key keeps eps = 2^-l across lengths d, d' <= D (Exercise 5.1). Single-word multiply-shift with odd a and no b (eq. 9) is only 2-approximately universal, eps <= 2/2^l (eq. 10); Thorup remarks that omitting b from (17) likewise drops the guarantee to 2/2^l. Proved (Lemma 3.6 / Fact 3.4), unconditional. The paper's VectorMultShift is the exact scheme (128-bit accumulate, 65 x 128-bit keys, keys from a PRNG, fixed length, cap 64 words).
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 64.00 -- formula eps = 2^-l with l = 64, w = 64, wbar = 128, fixed length d = 128 words (key 2(128+1) = 258 words); log2(1/eps) = 64.00. Odd-a single-word variant without b: 2/2^64 -> 63.00
rows.key_words: 2(L+1) 64-bit words for an L-word message (L+1 keys of 128 bits; 258 words at 1 KB; the paper's implementation holds 65 x 128-bit = 130 words at its 64-word cap). The paper table prints "L+1", which counts 128-bit keys, understating the resident 64-bit-word state by 2x against the caption's definition. 32-bit words to 32-bit output (wbar = 64): d+1 64-bit words for d 32-bit words. SMHasher3 resident state: multiply-shift / pair-multiply-shift 256 x 128-bit = 512 words (wraps every 256 message words); -32 variants 256 words
rows.output_bits: l <= wbar - w + 1: up to 64 with 128-bit multipliers on 64-bit words (paper row: 64); up to 32 with 64-bit multipliers on 32-bit words. SMHasher3: multiply-shift 64, pair-multiply-shift 64, -32 variants 32
rows.smhasher3: Registered upstream (hashes/multiply_shift.cpp, MIT, SRC_FROZEN, src_url rurban Hashes.cpp; copyright Wojcik 2021-2023, Urban, Ahle 2020, jason 2023). multiply-shift ("Dietzfelbinger Multiply-shift on strings, 64-bit blocks"): 18/250 passed (232 failed, 18 test families incl. all Seed*); multiply-shift-32: 20/250; pair-multiply-shift: 20/250; pair-multiply-shift-32: 24/250 (17 families, no Cyclic). rows.hash: Simple tabulation (Carter-Wegman 1977 / Zobrist; Patrascu-Thorup 2012) and twisted tabulation (Patrascu-Thorup 2013)
rows.bound: Exactly 3-independent (not 4-independent) for fully random tables T_1..T_c of l-bit entries and fixed-length c-character keys, h(x) = T_1[x_1] xor ... xor T_c[x_c]: any three distinct keys hash independently and uniformly, so eps = 2^-l (proof: some position i has a character x_i unique to one key). Twisted tabulation: also only 3-independent (eps = 2^-l) but with Chernoff-style concentration (SODA 2013). Proved. Fixed-length keys only; variable-length strings need a universe reduction first (Thorup Sec. 6, Exercise 6.1), and the 3-independence of the composition holds only conditioned on distinct signatures. SMHasher3's 'tabulation' is such a composite (multiply-shift block signature + Mersenne 2^61-1 polynomial combine + 8x256 tabulation finalizer, keys from splitmix per seed: "Hash quality is dependent on the RNG used!").
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 64.00 -- formula eps = 2^-l with l = 64 for fixed-length c-character keys; a 1024-byte key as c = 1024 8-bit characters needs 1024 tables x 256 x 64-bit = 262144 words (2 MB) of fully random entropy; log2(1/eps) = 64.00 (fixed length only; not the SMHasher3 composite's bound)
rows.key_words: c tables x 256 entries: 8 x 256 x 64-bit = 2048 words (16 KB) for 64-bit integer keys (paper Section 5.7 tabulation_64); 4 x 256 x 32-bit = 512 words (4 KB) for 32-bit keys; twisted tabulation 8 KB for 32-bit keys (Thorup CACM Fig. 1); 262144 words for a 1 KB string. SMHasher3 resident state: tabulation-64 = 256 x 128-bit multipliers + a,b + 8x256x64-bit tables = 2564 words (~20 KB); tabulation-32 = 256 + 2 + 512 ~ 770 words (6 KB)
rows.output_bits: l (entry width): 64 for tabulation-64 / paper tabulation_64; 32 for tabulation-32

rows.hash: Horner polynomial hash over GF(2^64) (paper rows "Horner, F_2^64" and "Horner, unrolled")
rows.bound: Almost-universal by Schwartz-Zippel: two distinct L-word messages give a nonzero difference polynomial of degree <= L-1 in the key x, so eps = (L-1)/|F| = (L-1)/2^64 (paper: "Horner's $(2n-1)/|\F|$ on the same $2n$ words"; Bernstein Sec. 4.2: the s-blinded authenticator m_1 r^n + ... + m_n r + s has forgery chance at most n/#k with r, s independent uniform, fixed n). Proved, information-theoretic, uniform key hidden from the attacker, fixed length per bound (variable length needs a length term). The paper's framework rows are fixed-length benchmarks; FW::seed() draws x uniformly ONCE per row (not per call) and the message words from getRandomUInt64. Paper score 64 bits (min_L log2(L*2^64/(L-1)) -> 64). Horner unrolled = same polynomial, Estrin-style 4-way grouping (x^2, x^4 derived per call), same bound.
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 57.01 -- formula eps = (L-1)/2^64 with L = 128 words: 127/2^64, log2(1/eps) = 64 - log2 127 = 57.01 (Bernstein's blinded form n/#k with n = 128 gives 57.00)
rows.key_words: 1 (x; the unrolled form recomputes x^2, x^4 per call)
rows.smhasher3: Not registered (the registered poly-mersenne.deg0..4 and polymurhash rows are different families).
rows.speed_m2_gbps: Sequential Horner: 1.3 (16 KB) / 2.3 (512 B); unrolled: 5.1 / 7.4 (speed_rerun.txt medians 1.2599/2.2638 and 5.0882/7.3794; public 3-pass run 1.281/2.295 and 5.162/8.153); framework implementations univ_horner_64 / horner_unrolled_64 (GF(2^64) via PMULL), Apple M2 Pro. Companion tab:injective:universal (us per 10^5 hashes, 2N = 8..256): Horner Seq 552/2109/7646/22976/64638/146944, Horner Unrolled 464/1045/2727/6684/13710/34503.

rows.hash: BRW (Bernstein-Rabin-Winograd polynomial over GF(2^64); paper row "BRW")
rows.bound: Almost-universal: for fixed n >= 1 the authenticator r H(m_1..m_n) + s has forgery chance at most (2n-1)/#k with r, s independent uniform (Bernstein Sec. 5.7); H maps k^n injectively to k[r] (Theorem 5.5), is monic of degree 2^{floor(lg n)+1} - 1 for n >= 3 (Theorem 5.4); about n/2 multiplications plus lg n squarings. Variable length only under Theorem 5.6's alphabet restriction (0 not in S, S and S+1 disjoint) or a length prefix. Proved, information-theoretic, uniform key. Paper score 63 bits (min_n log2(n*2^64/(2n-1)) -> 63). Injective (BRW) vs bijective (Rabin-Winograd) distinction is made in the paper's related work; almost-universal, not k-independent.
rows.key_words: 1 (r; the lg n squarings r^2, r^4, ... are recomputed per call in the framework; "One could cache r2 , r4 , r8 , . . ., eliminating the squarings in favor of lg n variables.")
rows.smhasher3: Not registered; no maintained standalone BRW library located (the paper cites Chakraborty et al. (hardware) and Ghosh-Sarkar (software) for other BRW implementations).
rows.speed_m2_gbps: 6.0 (16 KB) / 5.3 (512 B) (speed_rerun.txt 5.9809 / 5.3312; public 3-pass 6.039 / 5.907), framework univ_brw_64, Apple M2 Pro; tab:injective:universal BRW 1237/2332/4481/8833/17548/34879 us per 10^5 hashes at 2N = 8..256. "BRW is slower than the unrolled, scanned and laned forms on either machine; it beats only sequential Horner from $2N=32$, the sequential recurrence from $2N=64$, and, on the M2 Pro, the tree form of Horner up to $2N=128$."
rows.reference: Daniel J. Bernstein, "Polynomial evaluation and message authentication", 2007.10.22 (as above), Section 5.7, Theorems 5.4-5.6, Section 5.8; underlying scheme Rabin and Winograd 1972. Paper table row "BRW~\cite{Bernstein:2011:RW} & 1 & 63 & 6.0 & 5.3" (injective.tex line 328); code tools/bench/framework/injective_hashing_arm.h univ_brw_64<N>.

rows.hash: poly-mersenne (SMHasher3 poly-mersenne.deg0..deg4: Horner over 32-bit characters mod 2^61-1 with the byte length as first character, degree-K random-polynomial finalizer, 32-bit output)
rows.bound: Code-comment claim only, not a published theorem: "This hash has collision probability len/p" (len = number of 32-bit characters including the length character = ceil(bytes/4)+1, p = 2^61-1). Strictly, the key a is drawn from [0, (p-1)/2) for lazy reduction, so Schwartz-Zippel gives len/2^60; the output is truncated to 32 of 61 bits, adding ~2^-32 (for deg0 the wrap effect 2^32/(2^61-1) = 2^-29 was measured in the paper's appendix); a and the finalizer coefficients come from a 64-bit seed via splitmix (2^64-member subfamily; "Hash quality is dependent on the RNG used!"). The finalizer's K-independence holds for the map of the 61-bit residue, not for the composed string hash. The Ahle-Knudsen-Thorup Mersenne paper (arXiv:2008.08654) proves single-word k-universal hashing, not this string hash. Credited "Copyright (c) 2020 Thomas Dybdahl Ahle".
rows.bound_bits_at_1KB: 32.00 -- the 32-bit output floors eps at 2^-32 (paper rule: eps floored at 2^-w for a w-bit output): eps = max(len/2^60, 2^-32) with len = ceil(1024/4)+1 = 257: polynomial term 257/2^60 alone would give 60 - log2 257 = 51.99 bits; total log2(1/(2^-32 + 257/2^60)) = 32.00
rows.key_words: 1 word a (< 2^60) + (K+1) finalizer words: deg0 1, deg1 3, deg2 4, deg3 5, deg4 6 (a second word b is drawn but never used); all derived from one 64-bit seed
rows.output_bits: 32 ($.bits = 32; memcpy of 4 bytes of a 61-bit residue)

table.notes:
CONVENTIONS. bound_bits_at_1KB = log2(1/eps) for one pair of distinct 1024-byte messages (l = 1024 bytes = 128 64-bit words = 8192 bits), computed literally from each row's formula with the constants named in the cell; where the output width w is below the bound, eps is floored at 2^-w as in the paper's rule. This is NOT the paper's 'bits' column, which is min_L log2(L/eps(L)) (eps floored at 2^-w; sections/injective.tex lines 265-269): dividing by L cancels the Schwartz-Zippel factor, so e.g. Horner scores 64 there but 57.0 here. Script: experiment/provable/assemble/bits1kb.py. SMHasher3 figures are upstream x86 results of SMHasher3 20251015-release-5035a923 (raw files last regenerated in commit ea0b94f9, 2025-10-16; the README footer lists three releases, so the attribution is inferred), small-key column = [1,31]-byte keys per the raw files, bulk = bytes/cycle @ 3.5 GHz normalisation; README bulk figures differ slightly from the raw 'Average' lines (README's own aggregation). ChainHash SMHasher3 figures are author-run on a fork. M2 Pro GB/s are the paper's tab:injective:adversarial (injective.tex lines 300-348, tabular 318-347): 'Throughput is single-threaded, for $16$\\,KB and $512$-byte messages', Apple M2 Pro. Poly1305/GHASH M2 numbers are indicative local OpenSSL measurements under a different harness, not paper figures. Every proven bound in the table is for an ideal uniformly random key; all shipped implementations (ChainHash splitmix64, Polymur from_seed, UMASH umash_params_derive/Salsa20, CLHASH xorshift128plus, HalftimeHash splitmix/romu or mt19937_64, SMHasher3 poly-mersenne/tabulation splitmix) hash with a seed-expanded subfamily the theorems do not literally cover; UMAC/VMAC/GCM add a block-cipher PRP/PRF term. The 8-lane recurrence bound (ceil(N/L)+L-1)/2^64 was taken from tools/bench/adversarial/speed_hashes.h lines 142-146, not from the checked records.

VERBATIM BOUND QUOTES (as in the checked records, with the checkers' corrections applied; pdftotext renderings flatten superscripts, e.g. '264' = 2^64).

ChainHash / injective recurrence (sections/injective.tex lines 41-43, LaTeX verbatim): "If two distinct messages induce distinct key polynomials whose \\emph{difference} has total degree at most $d$, the Schwartz--Zippel lemma gives collision probability at most $d/|\\F|$ over uniformly random keys. In the three-key family $P_n$ is monic of degree $n$ in $y$ with the message-independent top part $(z+u)y^n$ (see the end of the proof of \\Cref{lem:injective:coeffmap}), so the difference of two such polynomials has total degree at most $n$, and the family is $n/|\\F|$-almost universal on messages of $2n$ field elements: half of Horner's bound at half of Horner's multiplications, with three resident key words. In the single-key specialization $P_n$ has degree $3n+2$ and its three leading coefficients are again the same for every message, so the difference has degree at most $3n-1$ and the family is $(3n-1)/|\\F|$-almost universal with one key word." Theorem thm:ph:collision (appendix_chainhash.tex lines 231-238): "Fix $W$, $S$ and $n\\ge1$, and put $p=Sn$.  For every two distinct messages $m\\ne m'$ with $n(m),n(m')\\le n$ (equivalently: of at most $nB$ bytes each), \\[ \\Pr_{\\kappa,\\theta,c,\\tau}\\bigl[H_{\\kappa,\\theta,c,\\tau}(m)=H_{\\kappa,\\theta,c,\\tau}(m')\\bigr]\\;\\le\\;\\frac{p+2}{2^{64}}=\\frac{Sn+2}{2^{64}} . \\]" and (lines 240-243): "For the $256$-byte configuration this reads $(\\lceil\\ell/256\\rceil+2)/2^{64}$ for messages of at most $\\ell$ bytes, and for the $1$\\,KB configuration $(2\\lceil\\ell/1024\\rceil+2)/2^{64}$: $3/2^{64}$ and $4/2^{64}$ for messages of up to $256$ bytes, $4098/2^{64}\\approx2^{-52}$ and $2050/2^{64}\\approx2^{-53}$ for messages of up to $1$\\,MB." Main text (injective.tex lines 397-402): "The collision probability is at most $(p+2)/2^{64}$ for two messages of at most $n$ blocks, $p=Sn$ sub-blocks: $2^{-64}$ for the block level (the full-width XOR-universality of carryless NH, extended to last blocks of different pair counts by the length term), $p/2^{64}$ for the recurrence (the three-key bound above, with $p$ counting sub-blocks rather than word pairs) and $2^{-64}$ for the finalizer (\\Cref{sec:ph})." Theorem thm:ph:kwise (appendix_chainhash.tex lines 703-716; RENDERED: the source is an enumerate with \\item lines 709-715): "Fix $W$, $S$, $n\\ge1$, $p=Sn$, and $t\\le5$ pairwise distinct messages $m_1,\\dots,m_t$ with $n(m_i)\\le n$.  Let $\\mathcal D$ be the event (determined by $(\\kappa,\\theta)$) that the level-2 values $V_\\kappa(m_1),\\dots,V_\\kappa(m_t)$ are pairwise distinct, i.e.\\ that no pair suffers an $E_1$ or $E_2$ collision.  Then (i) $\\Pr[\\neg\\mathcal D]\\le\\binom t2\\,\\frac{p+1}{2^{64}}$; (ii) conditioned on any $(\\kappa,\\theta)\\in\\mathcal D$ and on any $\\tau$, the vector $(H(m_1),\\dots,H(m_t))$ is uniform on $\\F^t$: the outputs are independent and uniform, in particular $5$-wise independent; (iii) consequently, for every $T\\subseteq\\F^t$, $\\bigl|\\Pr[(H(m_1),\\dots,H(m_t))\\in T]-|T|/2^{64t}\\bigr|\\le\\binom t2\\frac{p+1}{2^{64}}$." The implementation derives $(\\kappa,\\theta,c,\\tau)$ from a $64$-bit seed with \\texttt{splitmix64}; the resulting $2^{64}$-member subfamily is not covered by the theorems (no pseudorandomness assumption is made or needed for the ideal-key statements; cf.\\ the counting argument of \\cite[\\S2.5]{lemire2015clhash})." Polymur (README.md lines 7-14, markdown verbatim): "It is **mathematically proven** to have a statistically low collision rate. When initialized with an independently chosen random seed, for any distinct pair of inputs `m` and `m'` of up to `n` bytes the probability that `h(m) = h(m')` is at most `n * 2^-60.2`. This is known as an almost-universal hash function. In fact PolymurHash has a stronger property: it is almost pairwise independent. For any two distinct inputs `m` and `m'` the probability they hash to the pair of specific 64-bit hash values `(x, y)` is at most `n * 2^-124.2`." extras/universality-proof.md (lines 106-119): "Since the polynomial `f_m(k) - f_m'(k)` is non-zero, we can ask how many roots it has. Over the finite field mod `p` it is well known a polynomial has at most the same number of roots as its maximum degree. The maximum degree of our polynomial in question is `14 + n / 7`. Thus it has at most that many roots when reduced mod `p`. But `m` and `m'` were chosen independently from our secret key `k`. So the probability that the polynomial `f_m(k) - f_m'(k)` happens to have `k` as its root mod `p` is at most `(14 + n/7) / |K|` where `K` is the set of all possible keys. Ignoring the negligible constant 14, and given that we have roughly `2^57.4` possible keys, this gives us an overall collision bound of Pr[PH(m) = PH(m')] <= n/7 * 2^-57.4 Pr[PH(m) = PH(m')] <= n * 2^-60.2" (lines 162-163): "Pr[H(m) = x  &&  H(m') = y] <= n/7 * 2^-121.4 Pr[H(m) = x  &&  H(m') = y] <= n * 2^-124.2". Assumption (proof line 3-6, link markup restored): "The proof below assumes that our secret key `k` was chosen uniformly at random from all possible `K`, which in [the readme](../README.md#no-weak-keys) is described to be roughly 2^57.4 possible keys. Furthermore, it assumes this random choice is independent from our input." Tweak (two-line C comment, README lines 71-72 / polymur-hash.h lines 52-53): "// mixing, allowing different outputs much faster than re-seeding. No claims are" / "// made about the collision probability between hashes with different tweaks."

UMASH (README, markdown verbatim): "UMASH provably avoids parameter-independent collisions.  For any two inputs of `s` bytes or fewer, the probability that a randomly parameterised UMASH assigns them the same 64 bit hash value is less than `ceil(s / 4096) 2**-55`." and "Combining the two hashes yields a [128-bit fingerprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerprint_(computing)#Virtual_uniqueness) that collides pairs of `s`-or-fewer-byte inputs with probability less than `ceil(s / 2**26)**2 * 2**-83`; that's less than `2**-70` (`1e-21`) for up to 5 GiB of data." Whitepaper (umash_reference.py lines 45-71): "UMASH should not be used for cryptographic purposes, especially not against adversaries that can exploit side-channels or adapt to the hashed outputs, but it does provide worst-case pair-wise collision bounds. For any two strings of $s$ bytes or fewer, the probability of them hashing to the same value satisfies $\\varepsilon < \\lceil s / 4096\\rceil \\cdot 2^{-55},$ as long as the independently generated key is chosen uniformly at random." and "UMASH may also generate a 128-bit fingerprint by computing a secondary hash value concurrently with the usual (primary) UMASH value; the combination of the two 64-bit values guarantees a collision probability less than $2^{-83}$ for input size up to 64 MB, and less than $2^{-70}$ at 5 GB." Short inputs (source form, lines 79-81): "...collides values with probability $\\varepsilon_{\\textrm{short}} \\approx 2^{-64}.$" Key assumption: "The universal collision bounds for UMASH hold under the assumption that keys are fully re-generated with random bytes, independently of the hash function's inputs. While UMASH accepts a 64-bit \"seed\" value, it is merely a hint that we would like to see different hash values, without any guarantee. Nevertheless, this suffices to pass SMHasher's seed-based collision tests.  For real guarantees, expand short keys into full UMASH keys with a stream cipher like Salsa20." Rounding: "let's conservatively bump that to $\\varepsilon < 2^{-55}$ to take into account the block compressor's collisions and the rounding error from $2^{61} - 1 < 2^{61}.$ Longer strings will follow the same progression, so we can claim a collision probability $\\varepsilon < \\lceil s/4096\\rceil \\cdot 2^{-55}.$" 2020 blog (superseded; MathJax delimiters as in source): "while guaranteeing that two distinct inputs of at most \\(s\\) bytes collide with probability less than \\(\\lceil s / 2048 \\rceil \\cdot 2^{-56}\\)."

CLHASH (arXiv:1503.03465v8, pdftotext): "Lemma 9 CLHASH is 2.004/264 -almost XOR universal over strings of up to 264 bytes. Moreover, it is XOR universal over strings of no more than 1 kB." Derivation: "Thus, we have the composition of three hash functions with collision probabilities 1/264 , (n − 1)/2126 and 1/264 . It is reasonable to bound the string length by 264 bytes: n ≤ 264 /1024 = 254 . We have that 2/264 + (254 − 1)/2126 < 2.004/264 . Thus, for same-length strings, we have 2.004/264 -almost XOR universality." and "We further ensure that the result is XOR-universal over all strings: P (h(s) = h(s0 ) ⊕ c) ≤ 1/264 irrespective of whether |s| = |s0 |." Section 2 definition (parenthetical restored): "A family is -almost XOR-universal if P (h(x) = h(x0 ) ⊕ c) ≤  for any integer constant c ∈ [0, 2L ) and any x, x0 ∈ X such that x 6= x0 (where ⊕ is the bitwise XOR). A family that is 1/2L -almost XOR-universal is said to be XORuniversal [37]." Table 4 (RECONSTRUCTED from the flattened table, not a verbatim quote): CLHASH column: 1-1024 bytes: XOR universal; 1025-2^64 bytes: 2.004/2^64-almost XOR universal; VHASH column: 1-2^59 bytes: 1/2^61-almost Delta-universal. Section 5.1: "One might wonder whether using 1 kB of random bits is necessary. For strings of no more than 1 kB, CLHASH is XOR universal. Stinson showed that in such cases, we need the number of random bits to match the input length [37]. That is, we need at least 1 kB to achieve XOR universality over strings having 1 kB. Hence, CLHASH makes nearly optimal use of the random bits." Lemma 5 (source spacing, pdftotext lines 562-570): "Lemma 5 Given an even number m, the family of functions / of the form / h(x1 , x2 , . . . , xm ) =(a1 + x1 )(a2 + x2 ) / + (a3 + x3 )(a4 + x4 ) / + ··· / + (am−1 + xm−1 )(am + xm ) / in a finite field (GF (pn )) is ∆-universal, providing that the / keys a1 , . . . , am are picked from all values of the field. In / particular, the collision probability between two distinct inputs is bounded by 1/pn ." Algorithm 4 keys: "Require: 128 randomly picked 64-bit integers k1 , k2 , . . . , k128 defining a 128-bit CLNH hash function (see Equation 7) over inputs of length 128 / Require: k, a randomly picked 126-bit integer / Require: k0 , a randomly picked 128-bit integer / Require: k00 , a randomly picked 64-bit integer". Poly1305 (Bernstein 2005, pdftotext p. 8, superscripts restored as in the record: the dump renders ⌈L/16⌉ as 'dL/16e' and 2^106 as '2106'): "Theorem 3.3. Let m, m′ be distinct messages, each having at most L bytes. Let g be a 16-byte string. Let R be a subset of {0, 1, . . . , 2^130 − 6}. Then there are at most 8⌈L/16⌉ integers r ∈ R such that H_r(m) = H_r(m′) + g. Consequently, if #R = 2^106, and if r is a uniform random element of R, then H_r(m) = H_r(m′) + g with probability at most 8⌈L/16⌉/2^106." Also: "The crucial property of H_r is that it has small differential probabilities: if g is a 16-byte string, and m, m′ are distinct messages of length at most L, then H_r(m) = H_r(m′) + g with probability at most 8⌈L/16⌉/2^106." Abstract: "The security of Poly1305-AES is very close to the security of AES; the security gap is at most 14D⌈L/16⌉/2^106 if messages have at most L bytes, the attacker sees at most 2^64 authenticated messages, and the attacker attempts D forgeries."

row.bound_quote: Recurrence (sections/injective.tex lines 41-43): "If two distinct messages induce distinct key polynomials whose \emph{difference} has total degree at most $d$, the Schwartz--Zippel lemma gives collision probability at most $d/|\F|$ over uniformly random keys. In the three-key family $P_n$ is monic of degree $n$ in $y$ with the message-independent top part $(z+u)y^n$ (see the end of the proof of \Cref{lem:injective:coeffmap}), so the difference of two such polynomials has total degree at most $n$, and the family is $n/|\F|$-almost universal on messages of $2n$ field elements: half of Horner's bound at half of Horner's multiplications, with three resident key words. In the single-key specialization $P_n$ has degree $3n+2$ and its three leading coefficients are again the same for every message, so the difference has degree at most $3n-1$ and the family is $(3n-1)/|\F|$-almost universal with one key word." ChainHash (sections/appendix_chainhash.tex lines 231-238, Theorem thm:ph:collision): "Fix $W$, $S$ and $n\ge1$, and put $p=Sn$.  For every two distinct messages $m\ne m'$ with $n(m),n(m')\le n$ (equivalently: of at most $nB$ bytes each), \[ \Pr_{\kappa,\theta,c,\tau}\bigl[H_{\kappa,\theta,c,\tau}(m)=H_{\kappa,\theta,c,\tau}(m')\bigr]\;\le\;\frac{p+2}{2^{64}}=\frac{Sn+2}{2^{64}} . \]" followed by (lines 240-243): "For the $256$-byte configuration this reads $(\lceil\ell/256\rceil+2)/2^{64}$ for messages of at most $\ell$ bytes, and for the $1$\,KB configuration $(2\lceil\ell/1024\rceil+2)/2^{64}$: $3/2^{64}$ and $4/2^{64}$ for messages of up to $256$ bytes, $4098/2^{64}\approx2^{-52}$ and $2050/2^{64}\approx2^{-53}$ for messages of up to $1$\,MB." Main-text form (sections/injective.tex lines 396-402): "The collision probability is at most $(p+2)/2^{64}$ for two messages of at most $n$ blocks, $p=Sn$ sub-blocks: $2^{-64}$ for the block level (the full-width XOR-universality of carryless NH, extended to last blocks of different pair counts by the length term), $p/2^{64}$ for the recurrence (the three-key bound above, with $p$ counting sub-blocks rather than word pairs) and $2^{-64}$ for the finalizer (\Cref{sec:ph})." 5-wise independence (appendix_chainhash.tex lines 703-716, Theorem thm:ph:kwise): "Fix $W$, $S$, $n\ge1$, $p=Sn$, and $t\le5$ pairwise distinct messages $m_1,\dots,m_t$ with $n(m_i)\le n$.  Let $\mathcal D$ be the event (determined by $(\kappa,\theta)$) that the level-2 values $V_\kappa(m_1),\dots,V_\kappa(m_t)$ are pairwise distinct, i.e.\ that no pair suffers an $E_1$ or $E_2$ collision.  Then (i) $\Pr[\neg\mathcal D]\le\binom t2\,\frac{p+1}{2^{64}}$; (ii) conditioned on any $(\kappa,\theta)\in\mathcal D$ and on any $\tau$, the vector $(H(m_1),\dots,H(m_t))$ is uniform on $\F^t$: the outputs are independent and uniform, in particular $5$-wise independent; (iii) consequently, for every $T\subseteq\F^t$, $\bigl|\Pr[(H(m_1),\dots,H(m_t))\in T]-|T|/2^{64t}\bigr|\le\binom t2\frac{p+1}{2^{64}}$."

row.bound_formula: Three-key recurrence: eps = n / |F| = n / 2^64 for messages of 2n field elements (n = number of (a_i,b_i) pairs = L/2 for L 64-bit words); bits = log2(L/eps) = 65 -> floored at output width, table lists 64. Single-key specialization: eps = (3n-1)/2^64 with one key word. ChainHash: eps = (p+2)/2^64 = (S*n+2)/2^64 for two messages of at most n blocks of B = 8W bytes, p = S*n sub-blocks; 256-byte config (W=32,S=1): eps = (ceil(l/256)+2)/2^64 for messages of at most l bytes; 1 KB config (W=128,S=2): eps = (2*ceil(l/1024)+2)/2^64; 64-byte config (W=8,S=1): eps = (ceil(l/64)+2)/2^64. In words L = l/8: 256 B -> (ceil(L/32)+2)/2^64, i.e. about L/32 * 2^-64 for long messages, so bits = min_L log2(L/eps) = 62 as the table states (the minimum is hit at short L where the +2 term dominates). 5-wise independence: deviation at most C(t,2)(p+1)/2^64 for t <= 5 messages. Two-message collision under the k-wise statement: r + (1-r)/2^64 with r the level-1/2 collision probability (injective.tex lines 371-375).
row.proved_vs_assumed: Proved (information-theoretic, no computational or pseudorandomness assumption) for the IDEAL key: all key words independent and uniform on F = F_2[X]/(X^64+X^4+X^3+X+1). Recurrence: Schwartz-Zippel over uniform (u,y,z) after the injectivity Lemma lem:injective:coeffmap (explicit decoder). ChainHash Theorem thm:ph:collision and thm:ph:kwise: "the family indexed by a uniform $(\kappa,\theta,c,\tau)\in\F^{W+9}$" (rem:ph:gaps (A1)). CAVEATS verbatim from rem:ph:gaps (appendix_chainhash.tex lines 1099-1105): "\item \emph{Ideal key.}  \Cref{thm:ph:collision,thm:ph:kwise} are about the family indexed by a uniform $(\kappa,\theta,c,\tau)\in\F^{W+9}$ ($8(W+9)$ random bytes; $328$, $1{,}096$ and $136$ bytes for $W=32,128,8$).  The implementation derives $(\kappa,\theta,c,\tau)$ from a $64$-bit seed with \texttt{splitmix64}; the resulting $2^{64}$-member subfamily is not covered by the theorems (no pseudorandomness assumption is made or needed for the ideal-key statements; cf.\ the counting argument of \cite[\S2.5]{lemire2015clhash})." and (A2): "\emph{Exact field arithmetic.}  \texttt{gfmul} is assumed to be the field product in $\F_2[X]/(\Pi)$ (irreducibility of $\Pi$: \cite[\S4.3]{lemire2015clhash}, re-checked in \texttt{tools/bench/chainhash/sanity.py}); the fast and reference multiplies are compared in test T7, and the fast hash against the bit-serial reference in tests T1/T4 of \texttt{test\_\allowbreak chainhash.cpp}. Equivalence of \texttt{chainhash.h} with \Cref{def:ph:hash} is tested, not proved." Table caption (injective.tex lines 312-316): "The ChainHash bounds (\Cref{sec:ph}) are proved for a key of $W+9$ independent uniform field elements; the implementation timed and tested here expands a $64$-bit seed with \texttt{splitmix64}, a $2^{64}$-member subfamily that the theorems do not cover (\Cref{rem:ph:gaps})." Also (injective.tex 380-381): "Both statements are for the ideal key of $W+9$ uniform words; the implementation derives its key from a $64$-bit seed (\Cref{rem:ph:gaps})." Message model (A6): byte strings, length XORed as a 64-bit value, so l < 2^64; bound is for messages of at most n blocks (both messages). The twist's benefit against SMHasher3 keysets is explicitly empirical, not a theorem (injective.tex 392-394: "whether the twist suffices for a given test suite is an empirical question, not a theorem"). No heuristic mixing step anywhere. Key expansion of the O(B) block key from a few seed words is an OPEN problem (injective.tex "Key expansion" paragraph: "We found no better attack, but also no proof; the security of unreduced NH under $k$-wise independent keys is an open problem").
row.key_words: Three-key recurrence: 3 (u,y,z); the paper table lists the 8-lane variant with 4 and the F_{2^89-1} variant with 5; single-key specialization: 1. ChainHash: W+9 64-bit words (W block-key words kappa, 3 recurrence keys (u,y,z), 5 finalizer coefficients c_0..c_4, 1 twist word tau): 41 words for 256-byte blocks (W=32,S=1), 137 words for 1 KB blocks (W=128,S=2), 17 words for 64-byte blocks (W=8,S=1). Quote (appendix_chainhash.tex lines 93-96): "$\kappa=(k_0,\dots,k_{W-1})\in\F^{W}$, $\theta=(u,y,z)\in\F^3$, $c=(c_0,\dots,c_4)\in\F^5$, and the twist word $\tau\in\F$ (\texttt{t\_in} in the code), all $W+9$ elements independent and uniform on $\F$ ($41$, $137$ and $17$ words for the three configurations above)." The SMHasher3 registration expands all W+9 words from one 64-bit seed with splitmix64 (chainhash.cpp lines 943-957).
row.output_bits: 64 bits (one element of F_{2^64}) for the recurrence over F_{2^64} and for all ChainHash configurations (SMHasher3 registration "$.bits = 64"). The F_{2^89-1} recurrence row outputs the full 89-bit residue (the paper notes the low 64 bits of an 89-bit Mersenne residue are not a safe output).
row.implementation: Reference implementation: https://github.com/thomasahle/fast-polynomials, directory tools/bench/chainhash/ (public; MIT license per README). Files: chainhash.h (46 KB, header-only C++17, "fast arm64 (NEON PMULL) implementation"; requires AArch64 PMULL/PMULL2 (+crypto), optionally EOR3 under __ARM_FEATURE_SHA3; NEON-only, does not build on x86: results README records "the harness does not build on x86 (`xeon/harness_build.log`: `../framework/multiplication_arm.h:9:10: fatal error: arm_neon.h`; `chainhash.h` and `speed_hashes.h` are NEON-only -- the x86 ChainHash implementation exists only in the SMHasher3 port)"), chainhash_ref.h (bit-serial portable reference), test_chainhash.cpp (T1-T9, 490,022 checks, run under -O3, ASAN and Guard Malloc via build.sh, "arm64 / Apple Silicon only"), sanity.py (Rabin irreducibility check of the modulus), verify5.py / exh5.c (degree-5 finalizer decoder certificate and exhaustive small-field check). Portable + x86 (PCLMULQDQ, _mm_clmulepi64_si128) + ARM (PMULL) backends exist in the SMHasher3 port: fork branch mr/chainhash of https://gitlab.com/lobais/smhasher3 (commit c7947d25 "Add ChainHash, a provably universal 5-independent 64-bit hash"), file hashes/chainhash.cpp (1228 lines, C++, BSD 3-clause header "Copyright (C) 2026  Thomas Dybdahl Ahle"), raw: https://gitlab.com/lobais/smhasher3/-/raw/mr/chainhash/hashes/chainhash.cpp. Backend selection (chainhash.cpp lines 87-92): "CHAINHASH_IMPL_X86 x86-64 PCLMULQDQ (_mm_clmulepi64_si128)", "CHAINHASH_IMPL_ARM AArch64 PMULL. Only used when the compiler ... (__ARM_FEATURE_AES / __ARM_FEATURE_CRYPTO) or SMHasher3 detected it (HAVE_ARM_AES)", "CHAINHASH_IMPL_PORTABLE bit-serial fallback; always compiles." All three backends give identical verification codes. Maintained: research code, last edits 2026-09-05/06 (single author); not a packaged library, no releases. The recurrence-only rows use tools/bench/adversarial/speed_hashes.h (vector-resident three-key recurrence, NEON) and the framework tools/bench/carryless_arm.cpp / carryless.cpp (ARM PMULL and x86 PCLMULQDQ).

row.notes: (1) Family type: the recurrence is eps-almost universal (Definition def:injective:universal, collision probability over the key), i.e. an almost-universal (not Delta-universal) family; ChainHash additionally has the qualified 5-wise independence theorem. The paper's table scores it 62 bits = min_L log2(L/eps(L)) with eps the proven bound. (2) Two things the blog table must not conflate: the theorem covers the ideal key of W+9 uniform words (328 / 1096 / 136 random bytes); every SMHasher3 number and every throughput number was measured on the splitmix64-seeded 2^64-member subfamily that the theorems explicitly do not cover (rem:ph:gaps (A1)); the code-vs-definition equivalence is tested (490,022 checks against a bit-serial reference), not proved (A2). (3) The three ChainHash rows in the paper table have keys 137/41/17 words; only the 64-byte configuration is anywhere near the 8-word "one cache line" budget, and the paper lists all three below the line "proven, key > 8 words". (4) The SMHasher3 numbers are author-run on a fork, not upstream-published; the upstream results README (releases up to 20260827-release-22-c378d845) and rurban's table do not list ChainHash. The fork's Xeon small-key figures 107.77/108.57 cycles are what the paper rounds to "108 and 109". SMHasher3's small-key average is over [1,31]-byte keys. (5) Discrepancy to flag for the checker: tools/bench/results/MANIFEST.md section 7 (row->log table) still maps the ChainHash rows to the superseded adjacent-pairing figures 61.7/40.5, 57.7/36.8, 26.6/27.4 and quotes injective.tex as saying "62 GB/s" and "26.6 against 23.8", whereas the committed injective.tex (since 370c3d1, 2026-09-06) says 69.3/39.2, 67.7/37.6, 27.5/29.4 and "69 GB/s", "27.5 against 23.8"; the strided_v2 README documents the new numbers as the mean of two harness runs. The uncommitted MANIFEST hunk in the working tree is unrelated (SipHash/poly-mersenne seeded-differential tier wording). (6) The single-key specialization (1 key word, eps=(3n-1)/2^64) is proved in the paper but is not one of the timed table rows; the "This paper" rows are the three-key form. (7) The seeded-differential test cited in the paper is the author's own contribution to the fork (branch mr/seed-differential, commit 5309a850), not an upstream SMHasher3 test. (8) arXiv id is still the submission id submit/8036575; cite as a 2026 manuscript / GitHub repo until announced.

bound_formula (bits explanation): 'bits = log2(L/eps) = 65 -> floored at output width, table lists 64' misstates the paper's rule. injective.tex lines 266-269 define bits = min_L log2(L/eps(L)) with eps(L) 'floored at $2^{-w}$ for a $w$-bit output'; the floor is on eps and does not bite for n/2^64 (n>=1). The 64 comes from the minimum over L: at L=1 word (one pair, n=1) eps=1/2^64 gives 64, while L=2n>=2 gives 65. Replace the explanation with 'min over L, attained at L=1 (n=ceil(L/2)=1, eps=2^-64)'.

row.family: PolymurHash (Polymur) 2.0 by Orson R. L. Peters (2023): a 64-bit almost-universal and almost-pairwise-independent hash; Carter-Wegman polynomial evaluation over F_p, p = 2^61-1, in 56-bit (7-byte) words with Bernstein's pseudo-dot-product ((k+m0)(k^6+m1)+...), followed by an unkeyed Murmur-style 64-bit permutation `mix` and the addition of a second secret `s` mod 2^64.
row.variants: Upstream API (polymur-hash.h v2.0): (a) `polymur_init_params(p, k_seed, s_seed)`: two 64-bit secrets; k = 37^e mod p with e derived from k_seed by rejection sampling so k is a generator of the multiplicative group and k^7 < 2^60-2^56 (key space ~2^57.4); s = s_seed ^ const. (b) `polymur_init_params_from_seed(p, seed)`: one 64-bit seed expanded via polymur_mix into both. (c) `polymur_hash(buf, len, p, tweak)`: 64-bit tweak added to the polynomial accumulator before mixing; "No claims are made about the collision probability between hashes with different tweaks." Registered in SMHasher3 as two variants: `polymurhash` (desc "Polymur Hash (using polymur_init_params_from_seed)", params re-derived from each SMHasher seed) and `polymurhash-tweakseed` (desc "Polymur Hash (using seed as tweak)", params fixed from seed 0 via polymur_init_params_from_zero, SMHasher seed passed as the tweak). rurban's smhasher registers one entry `polymur` (submodule pinned at v1.0). The paper's row is `Polymur (random k, s)`: polymur_init_params with two random words, tweak 0 (tools/bench/adversarial/speed_hashes.h struct Polymur).
row.bound_quote: README.md (lines 7-14): "It is **mathematically proven** to have a statistically low collision rate. When initialized with an independently chosen random seed, for any distinct pair of inputs `m` and `m'` of up to `n` bytes the probability that `h(m) = h(m')` is at most `n * 2^-60.2`. This is known as an almost-universal hash function. In fact PolymurHash has a stronger property: it is almost pairwise independent. For any two distinct inputs `m` and `m'` the probability they hash to the pair of specific 64-bit hash values `(x, y)` is at most `n * 2^-124.2`." extras/universality-proof.md (lines 106-119): "Since the polynomial `f_m(k) - f_m'(k)` is non-zero, we can ask how many roots it has. Over the finite field mod `p` it is well known a polynomial has at most the same number of roots as its maximum degree. The maximum degree of our polynomial in question is `14 + n / 7`. Thus it has at most that many roots when reduced mod `p`. But `m` and `m'` were chosen independently from our secret key `k`. So the probability that the polynomial `f_m(k) - f_m'(k)` happens to have `k` as its root mod `p` is at most `(14 + n/7) / |K|` where `K` is the set of all possible keys. Ignoring the negligible constant 14, and given that we have roughly `2^57.4` possible keys, this gives us an overall collision bound of Pr[PH(m) = PH(m')] <= n/7 * 2^-57.4 Pr[PH(m) = PH(m')] <= n * 2^-60.2" and (lines 162-163): "Pr[H(m) = x  &&  H(m') = y] <= n/7 * 2^-121.4 Pr[H(m) = x  &&  H(m') = y] <= n * 2^-124.2"
row.bound_source: README: https://github.com/orlp/polymur-hash (raw https://raw.githubusercontent.com/orlp/polymur-hash/master/README.md, lines 7-14). Proof: https://github.com/orlp/polymur-hash/blob/master/extras/universality-proof.md (raw https://raw.githubusercontent.com/orlp/polymur-hash/master/extras/universality-proof.md, lines 3-6 assumptions, 106-119 collision bound, 128-163 pairwise independence, 165-169 no formal verification). Local copies: experiment/provable/polymur/README_polymur.md and universality-proof.md.
row.bound_formula: eps(n bytes) <= (14 + n/7)/|K| with |K| = totient(2^61-2)*(2^60-2^56)/(2^61-1) ~= 2^57.4; stated after dropping the "+14" as n/7 * 2^-57.4 = n * 2^-60.2 (almost-universal). Pairwise: Pr[H(m)=x and H(m')=y] <= (n/7) * 2^-57.4 * 2^-64 = n/7 * 2^-121.4 = n * 2^-124.2 (almost pairwise independent; needs s uniform on 2^64). In 64-bit words L (n = 8L bytes): eps(L) <= 8L * 2^-60.2 = L * 2^-57.2, so the paper's score log2(L/eps(L)) = 57.2, printed as 57 in tab:injective:adversarial.
row.proved_vs_assumed: Proved (informal written proof, extras/universality-proof.md): the message-to-polynomial map is injective (block-Horner encoding in 49-byte blocks plus three length-dependent tail polynomials; length recoverable from the top exponent and the k^1 coefficient); the difference of two distinct messages' polynomials is non-zero of degree <= 14 + n/7, so has at most that many roots mod p = 2^61-1; the finalizer `mix` (bijection) + s is invertible and adds no collisions. Assumed: "The proof below assumes that our secret key `k` was chosen uniformly at random from all possible `K`, which in the readme is described to be roughly 2^57.4 possible keys. Furthermore, it assumes this random choice is independent from our input." For pairwise independence additionally "that `s` is chosen uniformly at random from all 64-bit integers" (README: "The proof of almost universality applies to both, but for the proof of almost pairwise independence to hold you must provide 128 bits of entropy."). Caveats stated by the author: (i) the "+14" degree constant is dropped ("Ignoring the negligible constant 14"); (ii) "No claims are made about the collision probability between hashes with different tweaks."; (iii) not collision-resistant against an adaptive attacker: "PolymurHash is **not** a cryptographically secure collision-resistant hash if the attacker can see (or worse, request) hash values at will."; (iv) "While I don't have a formal verification for PolymurHash, at the very least I have a simulation in `bounds-check.py` that proves that even in the worst case we appropriately reduce `mod p` when necessary and that no overflows occur." Not covered by the proof: polymur_init_params_from_seed derives both secrets from one 64-bit seed (a 2^64-member subfamily; the README asserts the almost-universality proof "applies to both"); the SMHasher3 `tweakseed` variant varies only the tweak, which the proof does not cover. Weak keys are excluded by construction (k restricted to generators of the multiplicative group), which is what shrinks |K| to ~2^57.4.
row.key_words: Secret input: 2 x 64-bit words (k_seed, s_seed), or 1 x 64-bit seed expanded by polymur_mix; effective entropy ~57.4 bits for k plus 64 bits for s. Resident per-key state: `typedef struct { uint64_t k, k2, k7, s; } PolymurHashParams;` = 4 x 64-bit words = 32 bytes (README: "The initialized hash function uses 32 bytes of memory to store its parameters"). The paper's table counts key = 4 words.
row.implementation: https://github.com/orlp/polymur-hash -- header-only C (`polymur-hash.h`, header comment "PolymurHash version 2.0"), zlib license, plus test.c, extras/universality-proof.md and extras/bounds-check.py. Tags v1.0 (ffe06d32, 2023-06-20) and v2.0 (c6cc6884, 2023-06-23 "Changed behavior for the empty string, now depends on seed"); last commit a7cc6b00 2023-06-23 ("Add ULL suffix to reference values."), pushed_at 2023-06-23 -- no changes in three years, i.e. finished rather than actively maintained (361 stars at fetch). SIMD: none. README: "It is cross-platform, using no extended instruction sets such as CLMUL or AES-NI. For good speed it only requires native 64 x 64 -> 128 bit multiplication, which almost all 64-bit processors have." (uses __uint128_t, or _umul128/__umulh on MSVC). Author-reported speed: "On an Apple M1 machine it can hash any input <= 49 bytes in 21 cycles, and processes 33.3 GiB/sec (11.6 bytes / cycle) for long inputs." The paper's vendored copy source/fast-polynomials/tools/bench/adversarial/vendor/polymur/polymur-hash.h is byte-identical to upstream master.

row.reference: Orson R. L. Peters, "PolymurHash: a universal hash function with a proven collision bound", GitHub repository, version 2.0, 2023, https://github.com/orlp/polymur-hash (references.bib key `polymur`).
