row.notes: (1) The hint's "~2^-57" is the per-word form: n bytes * 2^-60.2 = L words * 2^-57.2; the README states the bound per byte (n * 2^-60.2) and the paper's 57-bit score is log2(L/eps) = 57.2. (2) The bound is a Schwartz-Zippel count over a key space of only ~2^57.4 (not 2^61) because seeding rejects non-generators and keys with k^7 >= 2^60-2^56; the proof drops the additive degree constant 14, so the exact statement is (14+n/7)/|K|. (3) Output is 64 bits but the polynomial stage is 61-bit; the 64-bit pairwise bound n*2^-124.2 relies on s being uniform on 2^64 (128 bits of entropy) -- with polymur_init_params_from_seed only 2^64 (k,s) pairs exist. (4) The README's "passes the full SMHasher suite without any failures" refers to rurban's smhasher (which pins v1.0; empty-string behaviour changed in v2.0) and footnotes issue #114 where Peters shows the Sparse low-32-bit collision test fails a perfect random oracle about 7.8% of the time. In SMHasher3 the from_seed variant passes 250/250 while the tweakseed variant fails 7 SeedBIC tests -- the tweak is exactly the mechanism the proof makes no claim about. (5) rurban's table lists no quality problems for polymur; its cycles/hash (41.68) and SMHasher3's (42.57 / 41.89) are on different machines (rurban "@ 3 ghz", SMHasher3 "@ 3.5 ghz", the SMHasher3 README names an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X pinned to 3500 MHz in its Performance section, not explicitly for the results). (6) Author speed claims (Apple M1: 33.3 GiB/s, 11.6 B/cycle, <=49 bytes in 21 cycles) exceed both the SMHasher3 bulk figure (4.02 B/cycle on x86) and the paper's M2 Pro figures (19.7 GB/s at 16 KB); the paper's number is a full-message call including seeding-free params, tweak 0. (7) The MANIFEST notes a second, later re-timing under load (harness_competitors.txt, 18.0 / 15.3 GB/s) that is "not used". (8) The upstream repo has had no commits since 2023-06-23; SMHasher3 tracks commit a7cc6b0 (v2.0 HEAD) and rurban's submodule tracks ffe06d32 (v1.0).

row.family: UMASH (Paul Khuong / Backtrace I/O): VHASH-style two-level hash — a bespoke 'OH' block compressor (PH carry-less NH over GF(2^64) mixed with ENH) on 256-byte blocks feeding a Carter–Wegman polynomial over Z/(2^61-1); short inputs (<= 8 bytes) go through a SplitMix64-based universal mixer; invertible xor-rot finalizer.
row.variants: (a) 64-bit hash `umash_full(params, seed, which, data, n)` with which=0 or which=1 (the two halves of the fingerprint; which=1 is 'as slow as computing a full fingerprint'); (b) 128-bit fingerprint `umash_fprint` = the two 64-bit values computed concurrently; (c) the 32-bit halves of the 64-bit output are also claimed to pass rurban/demerphq SMHasher. Not a parametric family in the message-length sense: block size 256 B and the 2^61-1 field are fixed. SMHasher3 registers four variants: UMASH-64 ("UMASH-64 (which == 0)"), UMASH-64.reseed ("UMASH-64 (which == 0, with full reseeding)"), UMASH-128 ("UMASH-128"), UMASH-128.reseed ("UMASH-128 (with full reseeding)"); '.reseed' derives a fresh full key from each test seed via umash_params_derive (Salsa20), the plain variants keep one global key derived from 0 and pass the test seed only as UMASH's 64-bit 'seed' hint. rurban's smhasher registers umash32, umash32_hi, umash64, umash128.
row.bound_quote: README (current): "UMASH provably avoids parameter-independent collisions.  For any two inputs of `s` bytes or fewer, the probability that a randomly parameterised UMASH assigns them the same 64 bit hash value is less than `ceil(s / 4096) 2**-55`." and "Combining the two hashes yields a [128-bit fingerprint] that collides pairs of `s`-or-fewer-byte inputs with probability less than `ceil(s / 2**26)**2 * 2**-83`; that's less than `2**-70` (`1e-21`) for up to 5 GiB of data." || Whitepaper umash.pdf / umash_reference.py (2022-02-23): "UMASH should not be used for cryptographic purposes, especially not against adversaries that can exploit side-channels or adapt to the hashed outputs, but it does provide worst-case pair-wise collision bounds. For any two strings of $s$ bytes or fewer, the probability of them hashing to the same value satisfies $\varepsilon < \lceil s / 4096\rceil \cdot 2^{-55},$ as long as the independently generated key is chosen uniformly at random." and "UMASH may also generate a 128-bit fingerprint by computing a secondary hash value concurrently with the usual (primary) UMASH value; the combination of the two 64-bit values guarantees a collision probability less than $2^{-83}$ for input size up to 64 MB, and less than $2^{-70}$ at 5 GB." and, for <= 8-byte inputs: "The result is universal, never collides values of the same size, and otherwise collides values with probability εshort ≈ 2−64 ." || Original announcement blog (2020-08-24, superseded numbers): "while guaranteeing that two distinct inputs of at most s bytes collide with probability less than \(\lceil s / 2048 \rceil \cdot 2^{-56}\)." and "a collision probability of \(\lceil s / 2048 \rceil^2 \cdot 2^{-112}\) (better than \(2^{-70}\) for input size up to 7.5 GB)."
row.bound_source: README: https://github.com/backtrace-labs/umash (raw: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/backtrace-labs/umash/master/README.md); whitepaper: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/backtrace-labs/umash/master/umash.pdf (source https://raw.githubusercontent.com/backtrace-labs/umash/master/umash_reference.py, lines 45-72 and 371-382, 398-406, 758-772); announcement blog: https://engineering.backtrace.io/2020-08-24-umash-fast-enough-almost-universal-fingerprinting/ (mirror https://pvk.ca/Blog/2020/08/24/umash-fast-enough-almost-universal-fingerprinting/); fingerprint update: https://pvk.ca/Blog/2020/10/31/nearly-double-the-ph-bits-with-one-more-clmul/
row.bound_formula: 64-bit hash: eps(s) < ceil(s/4096) * 2^-55 for two distinct messages of at most s bytes (current README/whitepaper). In 64-bit words L = s/8: eps(L) < ceil(L/512) * 2^-55, i.e. 2^-55 up to 512 words, then one more 2^-55 per 512 words. 128-bit fingerprint: eps_fp(s) < ceil(s/2^26)^2 * 2^-83 (= 2^-83 up to 64 MiB = 2^23 words; < 2^-70 at 5 GB). Derivation in the whitepaper: block compressor < ~2^-57, polynomial term 32/(2^61-1) ~ 2^-56 at 16 blocks (4096 B), 'conservatively' rounded to 2^-55. The paper's score bits = min_L log2(L/eps) = 55 (64-bit, at L=1) and 83 (128-bit). The 2020 blog stated ceil(s/2048)*2^-56 and ceil(s/2048)^2*2^-112 for the earlier fingerprint; the hint's '~2^-56' is that older figure.
row.proved_vs_assumed: Assumed: a uniformly random, input-independent full key. Verbatim (whitepaper/reference): "The universal collision bounds for UMASH hold under the assumption that keys are fully re-generated with random bytes, independently of the hash function's inputs. While UMASH accepts a 64-bit \"seed\" value, it is merely a hint that we would like to see different hash values, without any guarantee. Nevertheless, this suffices to pass SMHasher's seed-based collision tests.  For real guarantees, expand short keys into full UMASH keys with a stream cipher like Salsa20." The bound is pairwise almost-universality of the 64-bit output ("Its 64-bit output is almost universal"); the whitepaper proves it as a composition of 2^-64-almost-xor-universal PH, 2^-64-almost-universal ENH and a Carter-Wegman polynomial over Z/(2^61-1), by case analysis; the README calls it "a proof sketch for the collision bound" ("See `umash_reference.py` (pre-rendered in `umash.pdf`) for details and rationale about the design, and a proof sketch for the collision bound."). Not a peer-reviewed proof; no machine-checked proof. The final constants are rounded up by hand: "let's conservatively bump that to $\varepsilon < 2^{-55}$ to take into account the block compressor's collisions and the rounding error from $2^{61} - 1 < 2^{61}.$ Longer strings will follow the same progression, so we can claim a collision probability $\varepsilon < \lceil s/4096\rceil \cdot 2^{-55}.$" Fingerprint analogously: "Let's conservatively bump that to $\varepsilon_{fp} < 2^{-83}$ to take into account the other collision scenarios and the rounding errors from $2^{61} - 1 < 2^{61}.$" Caveats: non-cryptographic and linear — "once a few collisions have been identified (e.g., through a timing side-channel in a hash table), the linearity of the hash function makes it trivial to combine them into exponentially more colliding values." Practical keys come from umash_params_derive (a 64-bit value + 32-byte secret expanded by Salsa20) or umash_params_prepare on random bytes (may fail "less than `2**-100`"); derived keys are a pseudo-random subfamily, not the uniform key of the theorem (same gap the paper notes for its own seeded ChainHash). Key = 38 x 64-bit words (struct umash_params: uint64_t poly[2][2] + uint64_t oh[UMASH_OH_PARAM_COUNT + UMASH_OH_TWISTING_COUNT] with enum { UMASH_OH_PARAM_COUNT = 32, UMASH_OH_TWISTING_COUNT = 2 }; 34 of them (poly[0] + oh[0..31]) are used by the which==0 64-bit hash, all 38 by the fingerprint). Output 64 bits (hash) / 128 bits (fingerprint).
row.key_words: 38 (struct umash_params = 4 polynomial words {f^2,f} x2 + 32 OH words + 2 twisting words = 304 bytes; the which==0 64-bit hash reads 34 of them; the paper's table charges 38 to both rows)

Maintained: repo not archived, algorithm "finalized"/"frozen" ("STATUS: the hash and fingerprint algorithms are finalized, and so is the mapping from `umash_params_derive` inputs to UMASH parameters. However, the ABI is not finalized"), last push 2026-01-11 (test-infra housekeeping commits 9709e112/e6a28245/c052ad19), no GitHub releases/tags, 161 stars. row.notes: (1) The hint's numbers are the 2020 blog figures; the current README and the 2022 whitepaper state ceil(s/4096)*2^-55 for the 64-bit hash (not 2^-56) and ceil(s/2^26)^2*2^-83 for the fingerprint, with 2^-70 reached only 'at 5 GB'; for a blog table the honest 128-bit figure is 2^-83 (up to 64 MiB). (2) Bound type: almost-universal (pairwise collision), not XOR- or Delta-universal at the output; the internal PH layer is 2^-64-almost-xor-universal. (3) The SMHasher3 failures are dominated by Seed* tests, a direct consequence of the seed being a non-guaranteed hint; with full reseeding the remaining ~36 failures are BIC, Sparse, Permutation, Bitflip, Zeroes (and TwoBytes for 128-bit) — the algorithm is frozen, so these will not change. rurban's suite (which the authors tuned for) shows no quality problems. (4) SMHasher3 README shows 41.73 avg cycles vs 41.74 in the raw file (README rounding); the bulk figure 6.09 B/cycle = 19.86 GiB/s @ 3.5 GHz on SMHasher3's x86 host, whereas the paper's M2 Pro numbers use the aarch64 PMULL build. row.family: CLHASH (Lemire and Kaser): CLNH carry-less multilinear inner hash on 128-word (1 KB) blocks, composed with a polynomial hash over GF(2^127) (irreducible 2^127+2+1, lazy reduction) and a CLNH 128-to-64-bit reduction mod the irreducible 2^64+27, plus a length term k''*|M|. Almost-XOR-universal (equivalently almost-Delta-universal in a binary field); XOR-universal for inputs up to 1 KB.
row.variants: (1) CLHASH, 64-bit output, the family of Lemma 9 / Algorithm 4 (reference code `clhash()` default build; SMHasher3 name "CLhash", registered as "Carryless multiplication hash, without -DBITMIX"). (2) CLHASH with BITMIX: the same hash followed by the MurmurHash fmix64 bijection (compile option CLHASH_BITMIX; SMHasher3 "CLhash.bitmix"; the build rurban tests, his log header reads `carry-less mult. hash -DBITMIX`); paper: "A bijection does not affect collision bounds." (3) CLNH alone, the fixed-length inner hash (paper eq. (7), Lemma 5): XOR-universal with epsilon = 2^-64 on same-length inputs, key = one 64-bit word per message word; this is the row "CLNH (fixed length)" the paper benchmarks on the M2 Pro. No 128-bit output variant exists.
row.bound_quote: "Lemma 9 CLHASH is 2.004/264 -almost XOR universal over strings of up to 264 bytes. Moreover, it is XOR universal over strings of no more than 1 kB." [pdftotext flattens exponents: 2.004/264 = 2.004/2^64, 264 bytes = 2^64 bytes]. Derivation, same page: "Thus, we have the composition of three hash functions with collision probabilities 1/264 , (n − 1)/2126 and 1/264 . It is reasonable to bound the string length by 264 bytes: n ≤ 264 /1024 = 254 . We have that 2/264 + (254 − 1)/2126 < 2.004/264 . Thus, for same-length strings, we have 2.004/264 -almost XOR universality." and "We further ensure that the result is XOR-universal over all strings: P (h(s) = h(s0 ) ⊕ c) ≤ 1/264 irrespective of whether |s| = |s0 |." Table 4 (CLHASH column): "1–1024 bytes: XOR universal; 1025–264 bytes: 2.004/264 -almost XOR universal" (VHASH column for comparison: "1–259 bytes: 1/261 -almost ∆-universal"). Definition used, Section 2: "A family is -almost XOR-universal if P (h(x) = h(x0 ) ⊕ c) ≤  for any integer constant c ∈ [0, 2L ) and any x, x0 ∈ X such that x 6= x0 . A family that is 1/2L -almost XOR-universal is said to be XOR-universal [37]." Section 5.1: "One might wonder whether using 1 kB of random bits is necessary. For strings of no more than 1 kB, CLHASH is XOR universal. Stinson showed that in such cases, we need the number of random bits to match the input length [37]. That is, we need at least 1 kB to achieve XOR universality over strings having 1 kB. Hence, CLHASH makes nearly optimal use of the random bits."
row.bound_source: Lemire and Kaser, "Faster 64-bit universal hashing using carry-less multiplications", arXiv:1503.03465v8 (4 Nov 2015), Section 5 "CLHASH", Lemma 9 and Table 4 (PDF p. 10); composition argument in the paragraph preceding Lemma 9; Lemma 5 (Section 4.2) for the CLNH block level, Lemma 2 (tuples), Lemma 3/4 (length term). Same text in J. Cryptographic Engineering 6(3):171-185 (2016), DOI 10.1007/s13389-015-0110-5. URLs: https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03465 , https://arxiv.org/pdf/1503.03465 . Local verbatim copies: experiment/provable/clhash/paper_bound_lemma9.txt (and clhash_arxiv.pdf, clhash_arxiv_reading.txt lines 1030-1078).
row.bound_formula: For any c and any two distinct messages s != s' (lengths may differ), with |M| in bytes and n = ceil(|M|/1024) the number of 128-word blocks: Pr_key[ h(s) = h(s') xor c ] <= 2^-64 when max(|s|,|s'|) <= 1024 bytes (XOR-universal, exact); otherwise <= 2/2^64 + (n-1)/2^126 (block-level CLNH 1/2^64 + polynomial (n-1)/2^126 + final CLNH reduction 1/2^64), which the paper caps at 2.004/2^64 ~ 2^-62.999 for all |M| <= 2^64 bytes. In 64-bit words L: epsilon(L) = 2^-64 for L <= 128; epsilon(L) <= 2^-63 + (ceil(L/128)-1)*2^-126 for L > 128. The paper's metric bits = min_L log2(L/epsilon(L)) evaluates to 64 (minimum at L = 1), matching the table entry; for CLNH alone (fixed length) epsilon = 2^-64 at every length. The polynomial level uses k of degree <= 126 so the (n-1)/2^126 term is over GF(2^127) with lazy reduction mod (2^127+2+1)*2, which the paper states does not change the bound.
row.proved_vs_assumed: PROVED (Lemma 9, information-theoretic, no computational or independence heuristics) for the ideal key of Algorithm 4: "Require: 128 randomly picked 64-bit integers k1 , k2 , . . . , k128 defining a 128-bit CLNH hash function (see Equation 7) over inputs of length 128 / Require: k, a randomly picked 126-bit integer / Require: k0 , a randomly picked 128-bit integer / Require: k00 , a randomly picked 64-bit integer" -- all uniform and independent; the bound is over the key for attacker-chosen inputs. Proof chain: Lemma 5 ("Given an even number m, the family of functions of the form h(x1, x2, ..., xm) = (a1 + x1)(a2 + x2) + (a3 + x3)(a4 + x4) + ... + (am−1 + xm−1)(am + xm) in a finite field (GF (pn )) is ∆-universal, providing that the keys a1 , . . . , am are picked from all values of the field. In particular, the collision probability between two distinct inputs is bounded by 1/pn .") gives CLNH mod p XOR-universal on same-length blocks; Lemma 2 extends to tuples of blocks; the Horner polynomial over GF(2^127) with key of degree <= 126 is (n-1)/2^126-almost universal; a second CLNH reduces 128 to 64 bits; Lemma 3/4 add the k''*|M| term for different lengths. NOT COVERED by the theorem: (a) the reference implementation and SMHasher3 do not draw the 133 key words uniformly; `get_random_key_for_clhash(seed1, seed2)` expands two 64-bit seeds with xorshift128plus (a 2^128-member subfamily), and SMHasher3's `clhash_init` uses `get_random_key_for_clhash(s64, ~s64, ...)` from one 64-bit seed (2^64 subfamily); the paper itself generated keys with MT19937 for its SMHasher runs; (b) the reference code masks the polynomial key to degree <= 126 and re-draws a degenerate (0,1) pair, a negligible deviation from uniform; (c) the paper's SMHasher runs and speed numbers are empirical, separate from the bound. The paper also proves (Section 6) that plain CLHASH must fail the avalanche test because for inputs <= 8 bytes h(x xor y) xor h(x) = h(y), and offers the BITMIX bijection, which preserves the bound.
row.key_words: 133 64-bit words (1064 bytes): 128 words CLNH key + 2 words for the 126-bit polynomial key k + 2 words for the 128-bit k' + 1 word k''. Reference header include/clhash.h: `enum {RANDOM_64BITWORDS_NEEDED_FOR_CLHASH=133,RANDOM_BYTES_NEEDED_FOR_CLHASH=133*8};`; SMHasher3 copy: `CLHASH_64BITWORDS_CHUNK_SIZE = 128, CLHASH_64BITWORDS_EXTRA = 5`. The paper's own accounting (Algorithm 4 and Section 5.1: "using 1 kB of random bits") is 128*64 + 126 + 128 + 64 = 8510 random bits. For the fixed-length CLNH row in the paper's table the key is L words for an L-word message (the table prints "L"). Key is seeded from two 64-bit seeds (128 bits of entropy) in the reference API.
row.output_bits: 64 (single variant; CLNH inner value is 128 bits before the final reduction). SMHasher3 registers both variants with `$.bits = 64`.
row.implementation: https://github.com/lemire/clhash (CI badge now points at https://github.com/simdhash/clhash, the same code; GitHub API: license Apache-2.0, language C, not archived, 292 stars, created 2016-04-25, pushed_at 2026-05-23T01:43:10Z, latest commit c35030af "minor refactor (pedantic)" 2026-05-23). MAINTAINED: yes, active in 2026 (CMake package, install rules, ARM port, known-answer test tests/unit.c). Language: C99 single source file src/clhash.c + include/clhash.h, with a C++ `clhasher` wrapper (std::string/std::vector). README: "C library implementing the ridiculously fast CLHash hashing function (with C++ wrappers)"; "It has strong theoretical guarantees: XOR universality of short strings and excellent almost universality for longer strings."; "On a recent Intel processor (e.g., Skylake), it can hash input strings at a speed of 0.1 cycles per byte for sufficiently long strings." SIMD requirements (README "Requirements"): "On x64, you need PCLMULQDQ + SSE4.2 (Haswell from 2013 or later in practice). On older x64 chips it will either fail to build or be slow. The Makefile and CMake build pass `-msse4.2 -mpclmul -march=native` on x86." and "On 64-bit ARM (AArch64), you need the crypto extension that provides the PMULL/PMULL2 instructions (advertised via `HWCAP_PMULL` on Linux, and always present on Apple Silicon). The build passes `-march=armv8-a+crypto` on ARM." "POWER and other architectures are not currently supported; the build will fail at preprocessing with a clear `#error`." No AVX2 requirement. We include CLHASH (denoted CLNH) in our experimental comparisons as a throughput baseline." Caption: "Bits is $\min_L\log_2(L/\varepsilon(L))$"; "Throughput is single-threaded, for $16$\,KB and $512$-byte messages." Excerpt saved: experiment/provable/clhash/paper_m2pro_excerpt.txt.
row.reference: Daniel Lemire and Owen Kaser, "Faster 64-bit universal hashing using carry-less multiplications", Journal of Cryptographic Engineering 6(3):171-185, Springer, 2016, DOI 10.1007/s13389-015-0110-5; preprint arXiv:1503.03465 [cs.DS] (v1 11 Mar 2015, v8 4 Nov 2015), https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03465. Abstract (verbatim): "Intel and AMD support the Carry-less Multiplication (CLMUL) instruction set in their x64 processors. We use CLMUL to implement an almost universal 64-bit hash family (CLHASH). We compare this new family with what might be the fastest almost universal family on x64 processors (VHASH). We find that CLHASH is at least 60% faster. We also compare CLHASH with a popular hash function designed for speed (Google's CityHash). We find that CLHASH is 40% faster than CityHash on inputs larger than 64 bytes and just as fast otherwise." Bib key in the paper repo: lemire2015clhash (references.bib line 24). Companion benchmark code: https://github.com/lemire/StronglyUniversalStringHashing (paper footnote 5).
row.notes: (1) The paper's M2 Pro row is CLNH alone (fixed-length inner hash, epsilon = 2^-64, key = one word per message word), not the full variable-length CLHASH; the full CLHASH's 2.004/2^64 bound and 133-word key were not timed in the paper. Do not label the 27.3/26.3 GB/s as "CLHASH" without that qualifier. (2) Quotes from the PDF come from pdftotext, which drops superscripts: "264" = 2^64, "2126" = 2^126, "254" = 2^54, "261" = 2^61, "259" = 2^59, "x0" = x', "k0"/"k00" = k'/k'', and the epsilon symbol is lost ("-almost" = epsilon-almost). Verify against clhash_arxiv.pdf p. 10 before printing. (3) SMHasher3 numbers are for an x86-64 PCLMUL build only (the port is guarded by HAVE_X86_64_CLMUL); the local repo is the author's fork but results/README.md and results/raw/CLhash*.txt are byte-identical to upstream commit ea0b94f9. The 186-test failure count of plain CLhash is dominated by the avalanche/BIC/permutation-type tests that the paper itself predicts a linear-over-GF(2) hash must fail (h(x xor y) xor h(x) = h(y) for inputs <= 8 bytes); the BITMIX variant reduces this to 23. However both variants also fail collision-counting tests on inputs longer than 1 KB (Sparse 2/1280, 2/1536, 2/2048; SeedZeroes 1280 and 8448; TwoBytes 2048, 4096; Text Long alnum 1968-8272), e.g. raw/CLhash.bitmix.txt line 867 "Testing all collisions (      64-bit) - Expected        0.0, actual      13044", which a 2^-63 bound with a uniform key cannot produce; this points at the seed-to-key derivation used by SMHasher3 (`get_random_key_for_clhash(s64, ~s64)`) or the multi-block implementation rather than at Lemma 9, but I did not diagnose it. Similarly rurban's log (BITMIX build) shows "Keyset 'Sparse' - 96-bit keys with up to 4 bits set - 3469497 keys / Testing collisions ( 64-bit) - Expected    0.0, actual  41448" and PerlinNoise "Testing 16777216 coordinates (L2) : Testing collisions ( 64-bit) - Expected    0.0, actual 16773120"; rurban's README summarises the quality problems as only "PerlinNoise, machine-specific (x64 SSE4.2)". Flag this as an open implementation/harness question, not a disproof of the bound. (4) The reference code and both SMHasher harnesses draw the key from a 64- or 128-bit seed through xorshift128plus (the paper used MT19937), so the shipped hash is a small subfamily the theorem does not literally cover, the same caveat the paper repo applies to its own ChainHash rows. (5) The lemire/clhash repo carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE per the GitHub API; SMHasher3's copy is sublicensed GPL-3. (6) The paper also gives the composition constants 1/2^64 + (n-1)/2^126 + 1/2^64, so a length-parametrised epsilon can be tabulated exactly rather than via the 2.004 cap. (7) rurban table columns: MiB/sec 22932.36, cycl./hash 67.22, cycl./map 262.78 (2), size 1167 (row saved verbatim in rurban_excerpt.txt).

corrections: notes (3), SMHasher3 '>1 KB collision failures': WRONG ATTRIBUTION. Every failure the record lists on inputs longer than 1 KB (Sparse 2/1280, 2/1536, 2/2048; Text 'Long alnum' 1968-8272; TwoBytes 2048, 4096; SeedZeroes 1280, 8448) is a failure of SMHasher3's '---Analyzing differential distribution' pass, which hashes the XORs of consecutive hashes (tests/SparseKeysetTest.cpp:138 `testDeltas(1)`; util/Analyze.cpp:875-885, 949-954). The first-pass 'Testing all collisions (64-bit)' count is 'Expected 0.0, actual 0' for every one of those keysets in both logs (e.g. raw/CLhash.bitmix.txt line 859 for Sparse 1280 vs the delta-pass line 867 'actual 13044'). A delta collision is the four-input relation h(a) xor h(b) = h(c) xor h(d), which no (almost-)XOR-universal bound constrains, and it is the expected signature of the GF(2)-linearity of CLNH/polynomial hashing on sparse same-length inputs. Delete 'which a 2^-63 bound with a uniform key cannot produce' and 'fail collision-counting tests on inputs longer than 1 KB'. The ONLY first-pass 64-bit collision failure in either SMHasher3 log is Sparse 5/12 ('12-byte keys with up to 5 bits set - 64593561 keys', 'Expected 0.0, actual 2 (------) (^22) !!!!!', raw/CLhash.bitmix.txt 620-621, raw/CLhash.txt 622-623), a <=1 KB input where Lemma 9 promises 2^-64 per pair (about 1e-4 expected collisions for 6.5e7 keys); that single item is the open implementation/seeding question. Evidence saved in check-clhash/smhasher3_delta_evidence.txt.

variants (2) and notes (3), BITMIX scope: both the reference src/clhash.c (fetched 2026-09-17, check-clhash/upstream_clhash_c_excerpt.txt) and the SMHasher3 port (hashes/clhash.cpp lines 393-424) apply fmix64 ONLY in the short-string branch; the long-string branch (> 128 words = 1024 bytes) returns `simple128to64hashwithlength(acc, finalkey, keylength, (uint64_t)lengthbyte)` unmixed under either build. So 'the same hash followed by the MurmurHash fmix64 bijection' must read 'followed by fmix64 on inputs of at most 1024 bytes only'; CLhash.bitmix and CLhash are byte-identical on inputs > 1 KB, which is why the two SMHasher3 logs show identical numbers there (13044 / 30640 / 125824 delta collisions). This also qualifies the paper's 'we can slightly modify CLHASH so that all tests pass' (2015 SMHasher had no >1 KB delta tests).

proved_vs_assumed (b): 'masks the polynomial key to degree <= 126' is imprecise. Both the reference clhash.c and the SMHasher3 copy mask the top 32-bit lane with 0x3fffffff ('setting two highest bits to zero'), leaving a 126-bit value, i.e. degree <= 125; this matches Algorithm 4's 'k, a randomly picked 126-bit integer' but is one bit stricter than the Section 5 text 'degree(k) ≤ 128 − 2'. The re-draw is `while((a64[128]==0) && (a64[129]==1))` (reference) / `while ((key[128] == 0) && (key[129] == 1))` (SMHasher3), i.e. it excludes only the pair (0,1), which is a polynomial key of value 2^64 after the mask, not 'a degenerate (0,1) pair' in the sense of the zero key; state it literally.

bound_formula (refinement, not an error): the case split 'max(|s|,|s'|) <= 1024 bytes => 2^-64, otherwise 2/2^64 + (n-1)/2^126' is a valid but looser reading than the paper's. The 2/2^64 + (n-1)/2^126 sum is derived 'for same-length strings'; for |s| != |s'| the paper's k''·|M| term (Lemma 3/4) gives 'P (h(s) = h(s0 ) ⊕ c) ≤ 1/264 irrespective of whether |s| = |s0 |'. A tighter transcription: ε = 2^-64 if |s| ≠ |s'| or |s| = |s'| <= 1024 bytes; ε <= 2/2^64 + (n−1)/2^126 (n = ceil(|s|/1024)) for equal lengths above 1 KB; the 2.004/2^64 cap for |M| <= 2^64 bytes is unchanged.

All numbers in the record check out (2.004/2^64, 2/2^64+(2^54-1)/2^126, 133 key words = 128+5, 8510 random bits, 64/250 and 227/250, 48.19/7.36 and 60.80/7.33, 27.3/26.3 GB/s, 22932.36/67.22/262.78 (2)/1167, 292 stars, c35030af 2026-05-23, issue #3 open since 2016-12-31), as do Lemma 9, the derivation sentences, Algorithm 4 'Require' lines, Section 5.1, the BITMIX bijection sentence, the README requirement quotes, the SMHasher3 descriptions and flags, and the speed_assemble.py description. The remaining corrections are quote-fidelity issues (a dropped parenthetical in the Section 2 definition, a reconstructed Table 4 presented as a quote, normalised Lemma 5 typography, '60 %' vs '60%', truncations without ellipses), an imprecise description of the polynomial-key mask (126 bits, degree <= 125) and re-draw condition, the README.md-vs-ea0b94f9 provenance overstatement, and a tighter reading of the length-dependent bound. proved_vs_assumed is otherwise fair: the Lemma 9 chain, the uniform-key requirement, the xorshift128plus/MT19937 sub-family caveat and the avalanche explanation are all supported by the sources.

row.family: HalftimeHash (Jim Apple, 2021): tree hash over Z_{2^64} with NH (32x32->64 multiplies) at the nodes and a generalized Encode-Hash-Combine (erasure code of minimum distance k + NH + integer matrix T) at the leaves; no 64-bit widening multiplies, no finite-field arithmetic. epsilon-almost-universal (AU), not Delta-universal as a whole (its NH components are 2^-32-ADU).
row.variants: Paper variants by output size: HalftimeHash16 (k=2), HalftimeHash24 (k=3, the paper's headline), HalftimeHash32 (k=4), HalftimeHash40 (k=5); output = k words of 64 bits. Public C++ API (halftime-hash.hpp) exposes only HalftimeHashStyle512/256/128/64, each returning uint64_t: the k=2 (16-byte) core folded to 64 bits by XOR of byte-indexed random tables over the two output words and the length (TabulateAfter<V{4,3,2,1}<2>,2>). The Style number is the SIMD block width (512=AVX-512, 256=AVX2, 128=SSE2/NEON, 64=scalar), not the output width; the four styles are different functions (distinct SMHasher3 verification values). SMHasher3 registers them as HalftimeHash-64, HalftimeHash-128, HalftimeHash-256, HalftimeHash-512 ("Halftime Hash (64-bit blocks)" etc., $.bits = 64 for all). rurban's smhasher lists halftime_hash64/128/256/512.
row.bound_quote:
"The combined collision probability is
$2^{-32k}\left(2^{kp} + h^k + 1\right)$.
For HalftimeHash24, and for strings less than an exabyte in length, this is more than 83 bits of entropy." (Section "Cumulative Analysis", halftime-hash.tex l.500-504). Supporting statements: "A hash family $H$ is called is $\varepsilon$-almost universal (``$\varepsilon$-AU'' or just ``AU'') when \forall x,y \in D, x \neq y \implies \mathrm{Pr}_{s \in S}[H(s, x) = H(s, y)] \leq \varepsilon \in o(1)" (l.50-53); "HalftimeHash produces output that is collision resistant among strings of the same length. Adding collision resistance between strings of {\em different} lengths to such a hash family requires only appending the length at the end of the output." (l.128-129); "The height of the tree is thus $h \defeq \left\lfloor \log_f \lfloor n / b d w \rfloor \right\rfloor$." (l.462); "The tree hash is $2^{ k\lg h - 32k}$-AU." (l.465); "NH is $2^{-32}$-AU. In fact, it satisfies a stronger property, $2^{-32}$-A$\Delta$U:" (l.187-188); "In HalftimeHash24, \[(b, d, e, f, k, p, w) = (8, 7, 9, 8, 3, 2^2, 3)\]" (l.456); "$p$ & $2^2$ & $2^3$ & $2^3$" for HalftimeHash16/32/40 (l.383); "The codomain has size 16, 24, 32, or 40 bytes, and $\varepsilon$ varies depending on the codomain" (l.65).
row.bound_source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08865 (arXiv:2104.08865, submitted 18 Apr 2021); TeX source quoted verbatim from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jbapple/HalftimeHash/main/halftime-hash.tex (saved as experiment/provable/halftimehash/halftime-hash.tex; line numbers refer to it). Springer version: WADS 2021, LNCS 12808, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-83508-8_8
row.bound_formula: epsilon(n) = 2^{-32k} * (2^{kp} + h^k + 1), for two distinct strings of EQUAL length n (n counted in 32-bit words); k = output words = erasure-code minimum distance (2/3/4/5 for 16/24/32/40-byte output); p = largest power of 2 dividing any k x k determinant of the combine matrix T (paper: "2^2" for HalftimeHash16 and 24, "2^3" for 32 and 40); h = floor(log_f floor(n/(b d w))) = tree height, with b=8 (words per block), f=8 (fanout), (d,w)=(6,3) for k=2, (7,3) for k=3. Length dependence is only polylogarithmic (h^k). Worked number stated by the author: HalftimeHash24 (k=3) has epsilon < 2^-83 for all strings under one exabyte. Note the paper writes p as "2^2" but uses it as the exponent in 2^{kp}: with p=2, k=3, h<=16 (exabyte) the sum is 2^{-96}(64+4096+1) ~ 2^{-84.0} ("more than 83 bits"); reading p=4 would give 2^{-96}*8193 ~ 2^{-82.9998}, so the exponent reading is the one that matches the stated number. For the 64-bit-output implementation variants (k=2 core, p=2, then a 2^{-64}-universal simple-tabulation fold, composed by the Carter-Wegman lemma eps_F+eps_G) the derived bound is epsilon ~ 2^{-64}(2^{4} + h^2 + 2): about 2^{-59.3} at 1 MB (h=3) and 2^{-55.9} at 1 EB (h=16). This 64-bit figure is derived (by me and in tools/bench/adversarial/vendor/halftime_hash/PROVENANCE.txt), NOT stated in the paper. Different lengths: append the length (the implementation tabulates it into the fold).
row.proved_vs_assumed: Proved: epsilon-AU for equal-length inputs with the whole seed ("input entropy") uniformly random and the components "independently and randomly chosen" (EHC hashes "with independently and randomly chosen input entropy", l.211; k tree hashes "with independently-chosen input entropy", l.392). Ingredients are proved/cited: NH 2^-32-ADU (UMAC), Nandi's EHC eps^k-AU over a field, the paper's own Generalized-EHC lemma over Z_{2^64} (collision probability 2^{k(p'-32)} for the integer matrix T, Section 4), Carter-Wegman tree-hash and composition lemmas, Toeplitz reuse of the tail key (cited, not reproved). No assumption on the inputs (worst case over all pairs). Caveats: (1) the bound is for the k-word (16-40 byte) output; the only shipped API returns 64 bits via a tabulation fold, whose bound is a derived composition, not stated in the paper; (2) the length is not part of the proof -- "append the length" is asserted; (3) key must be truly random: the SMHasher3 port expands a 64-bit seed with splitmix/romu into the 70928-byte table and upstream's example fills it with std::mt19937_64 -- 2^64-member subfamilies the proof does not cover; (4) "with p \le 2^3" and the value of p are computed from the chosen matrices, no proof text for the determinant bound is given.
row.key_words: 8866 64-bit words (kEntropyBytesNeeded = 70928 bytes, compiled from the verbatim upstream header, commit caf7924: 6144 words of tabulation tables + 2722 words for the k=2 core sized for unbounded length). Paper's formula for the k-word variant: e*w + (f-1)*h*k + b*f*h*k + b*d*w + k - 1 words (l.506-511); "HalftimeHash24 requires 8.4KB input entropy for strings of length up to one megabyte and 34KB entropy for strings of length up to one exabyte." (l.512). Far above the paper's 8-word cache-line budget.

row.notes: (1) Naming trap for the table: the paper's HalftimeHash16/24/32/40 are output sizes; the code's Style512/256/128/64 and SMHasher3's HalftimeHash-64/128/256/512 are SIMD block widths, all with 64-bit output. The headline "83 bits" belongs to HalftimeHash24 (192-bit output), which no shipped API exposes; the shipped 64-bit fold is roughly 2^-59-AU at 1 MB by composition (derived, not in the paper). (2) The bound is for equal-length strings only; the paper says length-appending suffices and the code tabulates the length. Length n is in 32-bit words in the paper. (3) The p notation is inconsistent ("p = 2^2" vs 2^{kp}); the stated 83-bit number only works with p=2 in the exponent. (4) SMHasher3 "failures" are all in the differential-distribution sub-analysis (a linearity detector); hash-value collision counts pass everywhere. The paper's claim "HalftimeHash passes all correctness and randomness tests in the SMHasher test suite" (l.524) refers to rurban's smhasher of 2021, where halftime_hash64/512 still show no quality problems and halftime_hash128/256 carry "UB overflow"; rurban lists halftime_hash128 among "the fastest hash functions on x86_64 without quality problems". SMHasher3 (a different, stricter suite) fails all four. (5) Key size 8866 words is ~1100x the 8-word budget in the paper's comparison, and the seed expansion in SMHasher3 (64-bit seed -> table via splitmix/romu) is outside the proof. (6) rurban table (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G, https://github.com/rurban/smhasher): halftime_hash64 4801.79 MiB/s, 99.05 cycl./hash, 310.02 cycl./map, size 444, no quality problems; halftime_hash128 18220.34, 94.31, 307.50, 444, "UB overflow"; halftime_hash256 18249.32, 97.56, 322.85, 444, "UB overflow"; halftime_hash512 10906.18, 118.54, 326.76, 444, none. (7) No M2 Pro number exists; measuring it would need a new run with the vendored NEON-fixed header (the harness note says it was deliberately skipped). (8) The upstream repo is effectively unmaintained since 2022 and does not build on ARM without the one-line fix.

row.family: Poly1305 / GHASH: polynomial-evaluation (Horner) universal hashes used inside Wegman-Carter MACs. Poly1305 evaluates the message as a polynomial over the prime field Z/(2^130-5) at the secret point r; GHASH evaluates it over the binary field GF(2^128) at the secret point H.
row.variants: (1) Poly1305 (Bernstein 2005): H_r(m) = (m(r) mod 2^130-5) mod 2^128, 16-byte coefficients each padded with a 1-bit above the top byte; r is a 128-bit key with 22 bits clamped to zero (2^106 admissible values). MAC forms: Poly1305-AES (tag = H_r(m) + AES_k(n) mod 2^128, original paper) and the IETF one-time-key form in RFC 8439 (ChaCha20-Poly1305; tag = H_r(m) + s mod 2^128 with (r,s) a 32-byte one-time key). (2) GHASH (McGrew-Viega 2004, NIST SP 800-38D 2007): Y_i = (Y_{i-1} xor X_i) * H in GF(2^128) with polynomial x^128+x^7+x^2+x+1, H = E_K(0^128) in GCM. Two definitions: the designers' GHASH(H, A, C), which appends a block encoding len(A)||len(C) (this is the version the AXU lemma is about), and NIST's simplified GHASH_H(X) = X_1*H^m xor ... xor X_m*H, where the length block is instead appended by the GCM encryption/decryption functions. Output may be truncated to t bits in GCM (t in {128,120,112,104,96} and, with restrictions, 64/32).
row.bound_quote: POLY1305 (Bernstein 2005, Section 3, Theorem 3.3; pdftotext page 8, lines 375-381 of poly1305-20050329.txt): "Theorem 3.3. Let m, m′ be distinct messages, each having at most L bytes. Let g be a 16-byte string. Let R be a subset of {0, 1, . . . , 2^130 − 6}. Then there are at most 8⌈L/16⌉ integers r ∈ R such that H_r(m) = H_r(m′) + g. Consequently, if #R = 2^106, and if r is a uniform random element of R, then H_r(m) = H_r(m′) + g with probability at most 8⌈L/16⌉/2^106." Same section, lines 332-334: "The crucial property of H_r is that it has small differential probabilities: if g is a 16-byte string, and m, m′ are distinct messages of length at most L, then H_r(m) = H_r(m′) + g with probability at most 8⌈L/16⌉/2^106." Abstract (lines 13-17): "The security of Poly1305-AES is very close to the security of AES; the security gap is at most 14D⌈L/16⌉/2^106 if messages have at most L bytes, the attacker sees at most 2^64 authenticated messages, and the attacker attempts D forgeries." ||| GHASH (McGrew-Viega, eprint 2004/193 full version, Appendix A, Lemma 2; lines 626-628 of gcm-eprint-2004-193.txt): "Lemma 2 (GHASH is almost xor universal). The function GHASH is ⌈l/w + 1⌉2^−t-almost xor universal when its second and third inputs are restricted so that their lengths sum to l or fewer bits and its output is truncated to t bits." Proof core (lines 676-684): "There are at most p + 1 values of H ∈ G for which R(H) = 0 holds. [...] The probability that R(H) = 0 holds, given that H is chosen at random from GF(2^w), is (p + 1)/2^w ≤ ⌈l/w + 1⌉2^−w, when the cumulative length of the inputs is restricted to l bits." NIST SP 800-38D Appendix B (lines 1529-1532 of nist-sp800-38d.txt): "In particular, if n denotes the total number of blocks in the encoding (i.e., the input to the GHASH function in the definition of S in Secs. 7.1 and 7.2 above) of the ciphertext and AAD, then there is a method of constructing a "targeted" ciphertext forgery that is expected to succeed with a probability of approximately n/2^t." (Typographic note: the pdftotext dumps render ⌈L/16⌉ as "dL/16e" and 2^106 as "2106", superscripts lost; the wording above is otherwise verbatim.)
row.bound_source: Poly1305: D. J. Bernstein, "The Poly1305-AES message-authentication code", https://cr.yp.to/mac/poly1305-20050329.pdf, Section 3 "Security", Theorem 3.3 (PDF page 8); differential-probability sentence and MAC bound in the same section (PDF pages 7-8); key set with #R = 2^106 in Section 2 "Keys" (PDF page 3). GHASH: D. McGrew, J. Viega, "The Security and Performance of the Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) of Operation (Full Version)", https://eprint.iacr.org/2004/193.pdf, Appendix A "Properties of GHASH", Lemma 2 and its proof; AXU definition in Appendix B (eq. 13); Theorem 2 in Section 4.1. NIST SP 800-38D (Dworkin, Nov 2007), https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf, Sec. 6.4 Algorithm 2 (definition), footnote 1 p. 9, Appendix B (n/2^t forgery). Local copies: experiment/provable/poly1305-ghash/{poly1305-20050329,gcm-eprint-2004-193,nist-sp800-38d}.{pdf,txt}, index in EXCERPTS.md.
row.bound_formula: Poly1305: for two distinct messages of at most L bytes and any 16-byte difference g, Pr_r[H_r(m) = H_r(m') + g (mod 2^128)] <= 8*ceil(L/16)/2^106, r uniform over the 2^106-element clamped key set. This is a Delta-universal (differential / "almost-XOR-universal w.r.t. addition mod 2^128") bound, so it covers plain collisions (g=0). In 64-bit words (L_w = L/8): eps(L_w) = 8*ceil(L_w/2)/2^106 = 4*L_w*2^-106 for even L_w, i.e. eps ~ L_w * 2^-104; the paper's score bits = min_L log2(L_w/eps) = 103 (attained at L_w = 1, where eps = 2^-103; 104 for all even L_w). The 8 = ceil(2^130/2^128)*2 accounts for the mod-2^128 truncation of the 130-bit residue (the "#U <= 8" step); without truncation (full residue) the bound would be ceil(L/16)/2^106. MAC-level: forgery probability <= delta + (1 - C/2^128)^{-(C+1)/2} * 8*D*ceil(L/16)/2^106, < delta + 14*D*ceil(L/16)/2^106 when C <= 2^64. ||| GHASH: eps-AXU with eps = ceil(l/w + 1)*2^-t for inputs (A,C) of at most l bits total, block width w = 128, output truncated to t bits; with full output (t = 128), eps = (p+1)/2^128 where p = number of 128-bit blocks (the +1 is the appended length block), i.e. the hint's n/2^128 with n = blocks + 1. In 64-bit words (L_w): eps = (ceil(L_w/2) + 1)*2^-128 ~ (L_w/2 + 1)*2^-128; score bits = min_L log2(L_w/eps) = 127 (attained at L_w = 1, eps = 2*2^-128), tending to 129 for long messages. Truncating to t bits multiplies eps by 2^(128-t) (NIST: targeted forgery succeeds with probability approximately n/2^t).
row.proved_vs_assumed: Poly1305: Theorem 3.3 is an unconditional, information-theoretic statement about the hash H_r alone: it holds for every pair of distinct messages of length <= L bytes and every difference g, and the only randomness assumption is that r is uniform over the 2^106-element clamped set R (the proof is a root count of the nonzero polynomial m' - m - u of degree <= ceil(L/16) over the prime field Z/(2^130-5), Theorems 3.1-3.2, summed over the <= 8 lifts u of g). No independence or message-distribution assumptions. The MAC-level guarantee additionally assumes (i) AES_k is a PRP with distinguishing advantage delta ("There is, however, no hope of proving that delta is small"), (ii) nonces are unique ("it is not true if the nonce-uniqueness rule is violated"), and in RFC 8439 that (r,s) is a one-time key (poly1305-donna README: "The sender MUST NOT use poly1305_auth to authenticate more than one message under the same key"). Poly1305's differential bound with r reused across messages is exactly what the theorem proves (r "MAY be constant" in RFC 8439); only s must be fresh. ||| GHASH: Lemma 2 is unconditional for H chosen uniformly at random from GF(2^128) (proof: R(H) = 0 has at most p+1 roots), for the designers' length-appending GHASH. In GCM, H = E_K(0^128) is only pseudorandom, so the deployed bound adds the block-cipher PRP/PRF advantage (Lemma 1, Theorem 2). Caveats: (a) NIST's simplified GHASH_H without the length block "does not obtain all of the properties that are shown for the designers' definition of GHASH" (SP 800-38D footnote 1) -- as a stand-alone hash it must be used with the length encoding appended, otherwise zero-padding collisions across lengths are trivial; NIST: "GHASH is a keyed hash function but not, on its own, a cryptographic hash function. This Recommendation only approves GHASH for use within the context of GCM." (b) The GCM-level proof (Theorem 1/2) was found flawed by Iwata, Ohashi and Minematsu (CRYPTO 2012, eprint 2012/438): "We first point out that a lemma, which is related to the upper bound on the probability of a counter collision, is invalid." ... "Although the security bounds are larger than what were previously claimed, GCM maintains its provable security." The invalid lemma concerns the counter/IV derivation (Lemma 3, non-96-bit IVs), not Lemma 2's AXU bound for GHASH itself. (c) H = 0 (probability 2^-128) makes GHASH constant (Lemma 4 "h is unlikely to return zero"); short tags leak H progressively (SP 800-38D Appendix B/C, Ferguson 2005). Both hashes are Delta-universal/AXU, not merely universal; neither is k-independent.
row.key_words: Poly1305: the hash key r is one 128-bit value = 2 x 64-bit words as stored (106 bits of entropy after clamping: "r[3], r[7], r[11], r[15] are required to have their top four bits clear ... and r[4], r[8], r[12] are required to have their bottom two bits clear ... Thus there are 2^106 possibilities for r"); the MAC adds a 128-bit one-time pad s (AES_k(n) or the second half of the RFC 8439 32-byte one-time key), so 4 words per MAC key. Implementations keep only r (plus r*5/4 precomputations, ~2-4 words) -- Bernstein's stated design goal: "The timings in this paper do not rely on any pre-expansion of the 32-byte Poly1305-AES key (k, r); Poly1305-AES can fit thousands of simultaneous keys into cache". GHASH: hash subkey H is one 128-bit field element = 2 words (in GCM derived as E_K(0^128) from the AES key); fast implementations expand it per key: OpenSSL's 4-bit table path keeps 256 B ("256B") or 528 B per key (32-66 words), and the PCLMULQDQ/PMULL paths keep powers H, H^2, ..., H^8 (up to 16 words) for 4x/8x aggregated reduction.
row.output_bits: Poly1305: 128 bits ("the 16-byte unsigned little-endian representation of (m(r) mod 2^130 − 5) mod 2^128"); the internal residue is 130 bits and the truncation costs the factor 8 in the bound. GHASH: 128 bits (one GF(2^128) block); in GCM the tag may be truncated to t = 96..128 bits (or 32/64 under Appendix C restrictions), with the bound scaling as 2^-t.
row.implementation: Poly1305 reference: poly1305-donna, https://github.com/floodyberry/poly1305-donna (C, public domain; "quite portable implementations of increasing efficiency depending on the size of the multiplier available" -- 8/16/32/64-bit variants selected by -DPOLY1305_{8,16,32,64}BIT, the 64-bit one using unsigned __int128; no SIMD required; last commit e6ad6e0 2016-03-28, effectively unmaintained; "Optimized implementations have been moved to poly1305-opt"). Production: OpenSSL https://github.com/openssl/openssl crypto/poly1305/ (poly1305.c portable C in base 2^64/2^32/2^26; perlasm asm/poly1305-x86_64.pl with integer, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512F and AVX512IFMA paths -- header table "Skylake[-X] 1.13/+120% 0.96 0.51 [0.35]" cycles/byte for IALU/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512; asm/poly1305-armv8.pl with integer and NEON paths -- "Apple A7 1.86/+5% 0.72"; also armv9-sve2, ppc, s390x, mips, sparc; actively maintained, last push 2026-09-17). BoringSSL https://github.com/google/boringssl crypto/poly1305/ (poly1305.cc portable, poly1305_vec.cc SSE2/AVX x86_64, poly1305_arm.cc + poly1305_arm_asm.S 32-bit ARM NEON). Requirement: only a 64x64->128 (or 32x32->64) multiplier; SIMD (AVX2/AVX-512/NEON) optional for 2-3x. row.notes: (1) The hint's formulas check out exactly against the sources: Poly1305 8*ceil(L/16)/2^106 is Theorem 3.3 verbatim (L in bytes, r uniform over the clamped 2^106 set); GHASH "n/2^128" is Lemma 2's ceil(l/w+1)*2^-w with n = number of 128-bit blocks including the appended length block (SP 800-38D Appendix B states the matching attack side as "approximately n/2^t"). (2) For the blog table in the paper's "bits = min_L log2(L/eps)" metric (L in 64-bit words): Poly1305 scores 103 bits (104 for even L) with a 2-word key and 128-bit output; GHASH scores 127 bits (129 asymptotically) with a 2-word key and 128-bit output; neither depends on message length beyond the linear Schwartz-Zippel factor. (3) Both are Delta-universal (AXU), i.e. they bound Pr[h(m) - h(m') = g] for every g, which is stronger than plain universality and is what the Wegman-Carter MAC proofs use. (4) Model caveats worth a footnote: Poly1305's r may be reused across messages (RFC 8439: "r" MAY be constant) -- the theorem is for the hash with fixed random r; GHASH's key H is E_K(0) in GCM, so the deployed guarantee is computational, and the NIST stand-alone GHASH_H lacks the length block that the AXU lemma needs (NIST only approves GHASH inside GCM). The 2012 Iwata-Ohashi-Minematsu repair affects GCM's counter-collision term for non-96-bit IVs, not the GHASH AXU bound. Not fetched here but well known: Saarinen's cycling weak-key classes for GHASH (FSE 2012) and Ferguson's short-tag attacks (NIST ref [1]) -- both consistent with, not contradicting, the eps bound. (5) SMHasher3: neither hash is registered in any local clone or in the 20260827 results release; rurban's table has no row either (only poly_mersenne and polymur among "poly*" docs). If a registration is wanted, note that SMHasher3's harness expects a seedable 32/64/128-bit hash of arbitrary length; Poly1305 with r derived from the seed (clamped) and GHASH with H derived from the seed would both fit, with 128-bit outputs. (6) The paper's M2 Pro table does not contain either hash; the local OpenSSL numbers above (GHASH streamed 6.4-7.0 GB/s via PMULL; Poly1305 per-message 2.1-3.3 GB/s via NEON; poly1305-donna scalar ~1 GB/s) are on the same CPU model as the paper (Apple M2 Pro) but under a different harness (OpenSSL speed / EVP_MAC, per-message setup included for the EVP numbers, no pinning, machine not idle), so they are indicative only and should be labelled as such; they are consistent with OpenSSL's own cycles/byte tables (Apple A7: GHASH PMULL 0.58 c/B, Poly1305 NEON 0.72 c/B) at the M2 Pro's ~3.5 GHz P-core clock (about 6 GB/s and 4.9 GB/s respectively for the pure block loops). The `openssl speed` CLI in 3.6.4 has no standalone poly1305 algorithm name (-mac is not an option), hence the EVP_MAC C harness in bench/macbench.c. (7) DBLP was behind a bot check, so venue details come from cr.yp.to/papers.html (Poly1305, verbatim) and from the GCM eprint's own reference [20] ("INDOCRYPT '04, LNCS, Springer-Verlag, 2004"); LNCS 3348 is from memory of the INDOCRYPT 2004 proceedings volume and was not independently verified here.

row.family: NH / UMAC (UHASH) / VMAC (VHASH) — Black, Halevi, Krawczyk, Krovetz, Rogaway (CRYPTO 1999); Krovetz (SAC 2006); Dai & Krovetz (eprint 2007/338); RFC 4418; draft-krovetz-vmac-01
row.variants: (1) NH[n,w]: block of n w-bit words, key nw bits, output 2w bits; UMAC uses w=32, n=1024 (signed variant NHS in practice); VHASH uses w=64, n=16 (NH[16,64] mod 2^126). (2) NHT[n,w,t]: Toeplitz extension, t shifted keys, output 2wt bits. (3) UHASH/UMAC (RFC 4418): L1 = NH[1024 B key, 32-bit words] per 1024-byte chunk, L2 = polynomial mod 2^64-59 / 2^128-159, L3 = inner product mod 2^36-5 -> 32 bits per iteration; tags 32/64/96/128 bits (UMAC-32/64/96/128 = 1/2/3/4 iterations). (4) VHASH-64 / VHASH-128 (draft-krovetz-vmac-01, revised 2007): L1 = NH[16,64] mod 2^126 on 128-byte blocks, L2 = polynomial mod p127 = 2^127-1, L3 = (m1+k1)(m2+k2) mod p64 = 2^64-257; VHASH-128 = two VHASH-64 iterations with shifted keys. Original 2006 VHASH (SAC 2006) used p = 2^61-1 in L3 and p1 k1 + p2 k2. SMHasher3 registers VHASH (64) and VHASH.32 (low 32 bits); rurban registers VHASH_64 and VHASH_32.
row.bound_quote: NH (umac-full.txt, Theorem 4.2): "Theorem 4.2 For any even n ≥ 2 and w ≥ 1, NH[n, w] is 2−w -AU on equal-length strings." Remarks: "The bound given by Theorem 4.2 is tight: let M = 0w 0w and M  = 1w 0w and note that any key K = K1 K2 with K2 = 0w causes a collision." / "Although we do not require any stronger properties than the above, NH is actually 2−w -AΔU under the operation of addition modulo 22w ; only trivial modiﬁcations to the above proof are required." / Signed: "Theorem 4.5 For any even n ≥ 2 and w ≥ 1, NHS[n, w] is 2−w+1 -AU on equal-length strings." / Toeplitz: "Theorem 5.1 For any w, t ≥ 1 and any even n ≥ 2, NHT [n, w, t] is 2−wt -AU on equal-length strings." with "A function in NH[n, w, t] is named by a string K of w(n + 2(t − 1)) bits."  ||  VHASH revised (vhash-security-eprint-2007-338.txt): "Theorem 1. Let b be any positive multiple of 128, ℓ be any positive multiple of b and p = 264 − 257, then VHASH[b] is ε-ADU (for addition modulo p) over all binary strings up to length ℓ bits where ε = 1/262 + 1/(264 − 257) + (ℓ/b)2−115 ." / "Corollary 2. Let b be any positive multiple of 128 and ℓ be any positive multiple of b, then VHASH[b] is ε-ADU (for addition modulo 264 ) over all binary strings up to length ℓ bits where ε = 1/261 + 2/(264 − 257) + (ℓ/b)2−114 ." / Fig. 1 caption: "Fig. 1. The hash family VHASH is (2−61 )-ADU for all messages upto 262 bits, when K, k, k1 , k2 are chosen randomly and b = 1024." / "In the context of VHASH, w = 64 and nw = b = 1024, making NH[16, 64] a (2−64 )-ADU hash family. In VHASH, however, we always follow applications of NH with a modular reduction by 2126 . [...] Corollary 5 tells us immediately that NH[16, 64, 2126 ] is (2−62 )-ADU."  ||  VHASH original (vmac-sac2006-krovetz.txt): "Theorem 1. Let b be any positive multiple of 128 and let ℓ be any positive integer, then VHASH[b] is ε-A∆U over all binary strings up to length ℓ bits where ε = 2−59.9 + (ℓ/b)2−107 ."  ||  UMAC/UHASH (rfc4418.txt): "The theory of Wegman-Carter MACs and the analysis of UMAC show that if one "instantiates" UMAC with truly random keys and pads then the probability that an attacker (even a computationally unbounded one) produces a correct tag for any message of its choosing is no more than 1/2^30, 1/2^60, 1/2^90, or 1/2^120 if the tags output by UMAC are of length 32, 64, 96, or 128 bits, respectively (here the symbol ^ represents exponentiation)." and "Another result [2], when combined with [3, 6], shows that so long as AES is secure as a pseudorandom permutation, it can be used instead of a random function without significantly increasing the 1/2^60 forging probability, assuming that no more than 2^64 messages are authenticated."  ||  VMAC (draft-krovetz-vmac-01.txt): "The theory of Wegman-Carter MACs and the analysis of VMAC show that if one "instantiates" VMAC with truly random keys and pads then the probability that an attacker (even a computationally unbounded one) produces a correct tag for messages of its choosing is less than 1/2^60 or 1/2^120 when the tags are of length 64 or 128 bits, respectively (here the symbol ^ represents exponentiation)."

VHASH (original): Ted Krovetz, "Message Authentication on 64-bit Architectures", SAC 2006, Theorem 1 — http://krovetz.net/csus/papers/vmac.pdf. VMAC forgery bound: draft-krovetz-vmac-01 (April 2007) Section 1 and 6.2 — https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-krovetz-vmac-01.txt
row.bound_formula: NH[n,w]: eps = 2^-w, AU (and A-Delta-U mod 2^{2w}) on distinct EQUAL-LENGTH strings of 2w..nw bits (n even); signed NHS: 2^{-w+1}; Toeplitz NHT[n,w,t]: 2^{-wt} with key w(n+2(t-1)) bits. Independent of message length (up to the block of n words); bound is tight. VHASH[b] (2007 revision, b = L1 key bits = 1024, all messages up to l bits, l a multiple of b): eps = 2^-62 + 1/(2^64-257) + (l/b)*2^-115 (A-Delta-U mod 2^64-257), or eps = 2^-61 + 2/(2^64-257) + (l/b)*2^-114 (mod 2^64); with b=1024 this is <= 2^-61 for all messages up to 2^62 bits. Original 2006 VHASH: eps = 2^-59.9 + (l/b)*2^-107. UMAC (RFC 4418) forgery: 2^-30, 2^-60, 2^-90, 2^-120 per attempt for 32/64/96/128-bit tags (N/2^60 over N attempts) plus 3*delta_AES, messages < 2^67 bits, at most 2^64 messages per key. VMAC: 2^-60 (64-bit tag) or 2^-120 (128-bit), plus delta_AES, at most 2^64 messages per key, messages up to 2^64 bits.
row.proved_vs_assumed: PROVED (information-theoretic, unconditional): the NH, NHS, NHT and VHASH collision bounds hold for a uniformly random key (NH: "a random function in NH[n, w] is given by a random nw-bit string K"; VHASH: "choosing K, k, k1 and k2 uniformly at random from their domains"). Caveats: NH's bound is only for equal-length strings (Theorem 4.2), equal-length restriction removed at the UHASH/VHASH level by length encoding and the polynomial layer; the eprint says "small modifications to the original proof show that NH is (2^-w)-ADU over messages that are any multiple of 2w bits in length (but still no longer than nw bits)". The UMAC paper notes "Several variants of NH fail to preserve collision probability eps = 2^-w. In particular, replacing the inner addition or the outer addition with bitwise-XOR increases eps substantially." ASSUMED (computational): in UMAC/VMAC as deployed, all internal keys (NH key, polynomial key, L3 key) and the pads are derived from a 16-byte AES key via KDF/PDF, so the MAC forgery bound is 1/2^60 (+3*delta for UMAC, +delta for VMAC) where delta is the PRP-distinguishing advantage against AES; RFC 4418 6.1: "The core of the UMAC design, the UHASH function, does not depend on cryptographic assumptions: its strength is specified by a purely mathematical property stated in terms of collision probability, and this property is proven unconditionally [3, 6]." Nonce must never repeat within a key. The SMHasher3 registration uses a fixed key "abcdefghijklmnop" and a homegrown seeding (seed XORed into the polynomial key), a subfamily outside the theorems.
row.key_words: NH[n,w] key = n w-bit words = nw/64 64-bit words: NH[1024,32] (UMAC L1) = 4096 B = 512 words; NH[16,64] (VHASH L1) = 128 B = 16 words. UMAC/UHASH internal key (RFC 4418 5.1, iters = taglen/32): L1Key = 1024 + (iters-1)*16 bytes, L2Key = iters*24, L3Key1 = iters*64, L3Key2 = iters*4 -> UMAC-32: 1116 B (139.5 words); UMAC-64: 1224 B = 153 words; UMAC-128: 1440 B = 180 words; external key 16 B (AES-128). VHASH-64 (draft-01): L1 key L1KEYLEN = 1024 bits = 16 words, L2 key 128 bits = 2 words, L3 key 2 x 64-bit = 2 words -> 20 words = 160 B ("VMAC uses 160 bytes", SAC 2006); VHASH-128: L1 1024+128 bits = 18 words, L2 4 words, L3 4 words -> 26 words = 208 B. SMHasher3 vmac.cpp context: nhkey[16] + polykey[2] + l3key[2] = 20 words.
row.output_bits: NH[n,w]: 2w bits (64 for w=32; 128 for w=64); NHT[n,w,t]: 2wt. UHASH: 32 bits per iteration -> UMAC tags 32/64/96/128 bits. VHASH: 64 bits per iteration (range 0..2^64-258, i.e. Z_{2^64-257}); VHASH-64 = 64 bits, VHASH-128 = 128 bits. SMHasher3: VHASH = 64 bits, VHASH.32 = low 32 bits.
row.implementation: VMAC/VHASH reference: https://fastcrypto.org/vmac/ — files vmac.h, vmac.c ("VMAC and VHASH Implementation by Ted Krovetz (tdk@acm.org) and Wei Dai. This implementation is herby placed in the public domain." "Last modified: 17 APR 08, 1700 PDT"), plus vmac.py (Python); C, public domain; needs an AES (rijndael-alg-fst or OpenSSL); x86-64 path uses GNU inline asm for 64x64->128 multiply and 128-bit add (no PCLMUL/AVX), SSE2 intrinsics only for 32-bit x86 (VMAC_USE_SSE2 when !VMAC_ARCH_64); page and spec dated 2007-2008, effectively frozen (SMHasher3 marks the family SRC_FROZEN). row.notes: (1) Two distinct VHASH bounds exist: the SAC 2006 original (eps = 2^-59.9 + (l/b)2^-107, L3 mod 2^61-1) and the 2007 revision actually specified in draft-krovetz-vmac-01 and implemented in vmac.c/Crypto++/SMHasher3 (eps = 2^-61 + 2/(2^64-257) + (l/b)2^-114 mod 2^64, L3 mod 2^64-257); use the 2007 one. Note the "2^-61" headline requires the per-block term (l/b)2^-114 to stay small: at l = 2^62 bits and b = 1024 it is 2^-62, hence "up to 2^62 bits". (2) The MAC-level 1/2^60 (UMAC-64, VMAC-64) is looser than the hash-level 2^-61/2^-62 because of the Wegman-Carter pad and the mod-2^64 output conversion. (3) NH's 2^-w bound is per block and for equal-length inputs only; UMAC's deployed NH is the signed variant NHS with 2^{-w+1} = 2^-31 per 32-bit stream, which the paper says "helps explain the 2−30 and 2−60 forging probabilities". (4) The RFC 4418 text contains typos "1/^60" and "N/^60" in section 6.2 (quoted as printed); the cleaner statement is in Section 1 (quoted above). (5) Both reference implementations are frozen (VMAC 2007/2008, UMAC 2006); Crypto++ is the maintained VMAC. The WebFetch summary of the UMAC PDF failed on the raw PDF, so all UMAC quotes come from pdftotext of the saved PDF (umac-full.txt); the pdftotext rendering turns superscripts into plain digits (e.g. "2−w" = 2^-w, "1/261" = 1/2^61, "264 − 257" = 2^64-257) — quotes are verbatim as extracted. (6) rurban's smhasher table (fetched raw README): "| VHASH_32 | 13084.37 | 65.45 | 280.14 (2) |1231 | sanity, Seed, MomentChi2 |" and "| VHASH_64 | 13217.64 | 64.90 | 270.04 (2) |1231 | sanity, Seed, Sparse |" (columns: Hash function | MiB/sec | cycl./hash | cycl./map | size | Quality problems). (7) SMHasher3 numbers are x86 (results README, 3.5 GHz normalisation in raw), not M2 Pro. (8) OpenSSH's umac.c mention in "implementation" is from my knowledge, not a fetched quote.

bound_formula / notes(1): the "<= 2^-61 for all messages up to 2^62 bits" headline is attached to the wrong formula. With b = 1024 and l = 2^62, Corollary 2 (mod 2^64) gives 2^-61 + 2/(2^64-257) + 2^-62 = 1.75 * 2^-61 > 2^-61; it is Theorem 1 (mod p = 2^64-257) that gives 2^-62 + 1/(2^64-257) + 2^-63 = 0.875 * 2^-61 <= 2^-61, which is what the Fig. 1 caption states. Move the "with b=1024 this is <= 2^-61 for all messages up to 2^62 bits" clause to the mod-p (Theorem 1) formula, and in notes(1) change "at l = 2^62 bits and b = 1024 it is 2^-62" to "in Theorem 1 it is (2^52)*2^-115 = 2^-63 (2^-62 for the mod-2^64 corollary, whose total then exceeds 2^-61)".

variants(1) and notes(3): "UMAC uses w=32, n=1024 (signed variant NHS in practice)" and "UMAC's deployed NH is the signed variant NHS" describe the 1999 paper's UMAC-STD, not the standardized UHASH. RFC 4418 defines L1-HASH with unsigned arithmetic: "S +_32 T" as uint2str(str2uint(S) + str2uint(T) mod 2^32, 4) and "S *_64 T" as uint2str(str2uint(S) * str2uint(T) mod 2^64, 8) (rfc4418.txt l.311-313, l.719-722), and its L1Key is 1024 bytes (n = 256 32-bit words), not 1024 words. Reword to: 1999 paper UMAC-STD: NHS (signed), K = 1024 32-bit words; RFC 4418 UHASH: unsigned NH mod 2^64 on 1024-byte chunks with a 1024-byte L1Key.

key_words: "NH[1024,32] (UMAC L1) = 4096 B = 512 words" is the CRYPTO '99 paper's parameter ("K is 1024 words (a word being 32-bits)", umac-full.txt l.170-171); RFC 4418's L1Key is 1024 bytes = 128 words. Label the 4096 B figure as the 1999-paper UMAC and keep the RFC figures (1116/1224/1440 B) as UMAC-32/64/128 as deployed.

notes(2): "because of the Wegman-Carter pad and the mod-2^64 output conversion" is an unsourced explanation; neither RFC 4418, draft-krovetz-vmac-01 nor the eprint attributes the gap between 2^-61/2^-62 and 1/2^60 to those two causes. Either drop the causal clause or mark it as the record author's inference.

row.family: multiply-shift-tabulation (Dietzfelbinger multiply-shift / multiply-add-shift, vector and pair multiply-shift; Patrascu-Thorup simple and twisted tabulation)
row.variants: (1) Universal multiply-shift [Dietzfelbinger-Hagerup-Katajainen-Penttonen 1997; Thorup notes eq. (9)]: h_a(x) = floor((a*x mod 2^w)/2^(w-l)), a a uniform odd w-bit integer; 2-approximately universal, eps <= 2/2^l. (2) Strongly universal multiply-add-shift [Dietzfelbinger STACS 1996; Thorup eq. (16), Theorem 3.5]: h_{a,b}(x) = (ax+b)[wbar-l, wbar) with wbar >= w+l-1, a,b uniform in [2^wbar]; exactly 2-independent. (3) Vector multiply-shift [Thorup eq. (17), Theorem 3.7]: h(x_0..x_{d-1}) = (sum_i a_i x_i + b)[wbar-l, wbar), d+1 uniform keys in [2^wbar]; strongly universal, collision probability exactly 1/2^l for fixed-length d-word vectors. (4) Pair-multiply-shift [Thorup eq. (18), from UMAC/NH; Exercise 3.10]: sum over pairs (a_{2i}+x_{2i+1})(a_{2i+1}+x_{2i}) + b, same keys, one multiplication per two words; strongly universal. (5) Prefix pair-multiply-shift [Thorup eq. (20), Exercise 5.1]: variable length d <= D with the length-position key a_d added; strongly universal across lengths. (6) Simple tabulation [Carter-Wegman 1977 / Zobrist; Patrascu-Thorup JACM 2012]: key split into c characters, h(x) = T_1[x_1] xor ... xor T_c[x_c]; exactly 3-independent (hence eps = 2^-l), not 4-independent; with 8-bit characters c=4 tables of 256 entries for 32-bit keys, c=8 for 64-bit keys. (7) Twisted tabulation [Patrascu-Thorup SODA 2013]: one character 'twisted' by a tabulated twister; still only 3-independent but with Chernoff-style concentration; tables of 256 entries with double-width entries (8 KB for 32-bit keys). SMHasher3 registers: multiply_shift (64-bit), multiply_shift_32, pair_multiply_shift (64-bit), pair_multiply_shift_32, tabulation_64 (= 256-word multiply-shift block signature + Mersenne-2^61-1 polynomial combine + 8x256 simple-tabulation finalizer), tabulation_32 (same structure with Mersenne 2^31-1 and 4x256 tables). The paper's M2 row 'Multiply-shift (fixed length)' is variant (3) with w=l=64, wbar=128 (tools/bench/adversarial/hashes.h VectorMultShift); the paper's Section 5.7 'Tabulation' row is variant (6) with 8x256 64-bit tables on 64-bit integer keys (tools/bench/framework/fast_hashing_arm.h tabulation_64).

row.bound_formula: Vector / pair multiply-shift (proved): for w-bit words, l-bit output, wbar >= w+l-1, and d+1 independent uniform keys a_0..a_{d-1}, b in [2^wbar]: for any distinct fixed-length vectors x != y in [2^w]^d and any q,r in [2^l], Pr[h(x)=q and h(y)=r] = 2^{-2l}; hence eps = Pr[h(x)=h(y)] = 2^{-l} exactly, independent of the length d (Theorem 3.7; "collision probability 1/2^l"). With w=64, l=64 the theorem needs wbar >= 127, so 128-bit multipliers give eps = 2^-64 for 64-bit output (this is the 'bits = 64' entry in the paper's table: min_L log2(L/eps) = 64 at L=1). Dropping b (odd a only, w=wbar) gives the universal-only bound eps <= 2/2^l (eq. 10). Variable length: the prefix form (20) with the length-indexed key a_d keeps eps = 2^{-l} for any two vectors of lengths d, d' <= D (Exercise 5.1); byte strings of <= 256 chars without NUL map injectively into such vectors (Exercise 5.2). Key size: d+1 (or D+1) keys of wbar bits = O(message length). Simple tabulation (proved): with c characters and tables T_i of 2^8 random l-bit entries, the family is exactly 3-independent (any 3 distinct keys hash independently and uniformly), so eps = 2^{-l} for l-bit entries, for fixed-length c-character keys only; not 4-independent. Twisted tabulation: also 3-independent (eps = 2^{-l}) plus Chernoff-style concentration (Theorem 5 of arXiv:1505.01523, citing SODA 2013). Neither tabulation bound covers variable-length strings: SMHasher3's 'tabulation' first reduces the string to a 64-bit signature (multiply-shift blocks combined by a Mersenne-2^61-1 polynomial), and the 3-independence of the composition holds only conditioned on distinct signatures (Thorup Sec. 6, Exercise 6.1 'universe reduction').
row.proved_vs_assumed: PROVED (Thorup notes; original in Dietzfelbinger 1996/1997): exact strong universality (2-independence) of multiply-add-shift, vector and pair multiply-shift under the sole assumption that the key words a_0..a_{d-1}, b are independent and uniform in [2^wbar] with wbar >= w+l-1 (proofs by Lemma 3.6 / Fact 3.4, unconditional, no independence assumption on inputs, adversary chooses x,y before the key). The universal (no b) variant is proved 2-approximately universal for uniform odd a. Simple tabulation is proved exactly 3-independent for fully random tables and fixed-length c-character keys; twisted tabulation proved 3-independent with Chernoff-style bounds (SODA 2013). Message-length caveat: the fixed-length theorem (17)/(18) covers vectors of one length d; different lengths need the prefix scheme (20) or a length term. ASSUMED / NOT COVERED in the implementations: (a) the paper's VectorMultShift (tools/bench/adversarial/hashes.h) is the exact scheme (128-bit accumulate, 65 x 128-bit keys) but draws its keys from a PRNG (Rng::next128) and caps messages at 64 words; length is not encoded (fixed-length row only). (b) SMHasher3 multiply_shift (64-bit): keys are 256 x 128-bit words generated once at init from a Xorshift RNG with seed 0 (seedfn commented out), the SMHasher seed and len_bytes enter only as two extra linear terms, the key table wraps modulo 256 words so messages beyond 2 KB reuse multipliers, and the loop sums only the high 64 bits of each 128-bit product (source comment: "XXX This doesn't seem to quite match the paper, as we are only maintaining a sum of the high bits"), so the 64-bit SMHasher3 variant is not literally the proved scheme; the 32-bit variants (64-bit products, high 32 bits) follow (17)/(18) with wbar=64, w=l=32 within one 256-word key block. (c) SMHasher3 tabulation_64/32: keys from splitmix per seed ("Hash quality is dependent on the RNG used!"), 3-independence only conditional on the multiply-shift/Mersenne signature not colliding; registered badseeddesc "Many seeds can collide on keys of all zero bytes". (d) The paper's tabulation_64 draws 8x256 entries from getRandomUInt64() and hashes 64-bit integers only. Key size in 64-bit words (from the formulas): vector/pair multiply-shift, 64-bit words to 64-bit output: 2(L+1) words for an L-word message (L+1 keys of 128 bits); 32-bit words to 32-bit output: d+1 64-bit keys for d 32-bit words = 2L+1 words per L 64-bit message words. SMHasher3 resident state: multiply_shift/pair_multiply_shift 256 x 128-bit = 512 words (4 KB); the -32 variants 256 x 64-bit = 256 words (2 KB); tabulation_64 = 256 x 128-bit multipliers + a,b + 8x256x64-bit tables = 512+4+2048 = 2564 words (~20 KB); tabulation_32 = 256 x 64-bit + 4x256x32-bit = 256+512 = 768 words (6 KB); paper tabulation_64: 2048 words (16 KB). Output width: l <= wbar-w+1; SMHasher3 64 bits (multiply-shift, pair-multiply-shift, tabulation-64) and 32 bits (-32 variants, tabulation-32); paper VectorMultShift 64 bits.
row.key_words: Vector/pair multiply-shift, 64-bit message words to 64-bit output (wbar=128): L+1 keys of 128 bits = 2(L+1) 64-bit words for an L-word message (paper implementation: 65 x 128-bit = 130 words for its 64-word cap; the paper's table prints 'L+1'). 32-bit words to 32-bit output (wbar=64): d+1 64-bit words for d 32-bit words. SMHasher3 resident key state: multiply-shift / pair-multiply-shift 512 words (256 x 128-bit, wraps every 256 message words), multiply-shift-32 / pair-multiply-shift-32 256 words, tabulation-64 2564 words (~20 KB), tabulation-32 768 words (6 KB). Simple tabulation on 64-bit integer keys (paper Section 5.7): 8 tables x 256 x 64-bit = 2048 words (16 KB); 32-bit keys: 4 x 256 x 32-bit = 512 words (4 KB); twisted tabulation 32-bit keys: 8 KB (Thorup CACM Fig. 1).
row.output_bits: l bits with l <= wbar - w + 1 (any l up to 64 with 128-bit multipliers on 64-bit words; up to 32 with 64-bit multipliers on 32-bit words). Registered: multiply-shift 64, pair-multiply-shift 64, multiply-shift-32 32, pair-multiply-shift-32 32, tabulation-64 64, tabulation-32 32. Paper M2 row: 64 (table 'bits' = 64).
row.implementation: No standalone maintained library; Thorup's notes give inline C snippets only. (1) Paper (this repo): source/fast-polynomials/tools/bench/adversarial/hashes.h struct VectorMultShift ("Vector multiply-add-shift (Dietzfelbinger 1996), strongly universal"): C++17, unsigned __int128 accumulate acc = a[0] + sum a[k]*w_k, output acc >> 64, 65 x 128-bit keys, MAXW = 64 words; scalar 64x64->128 multiply, no SIMD, no PCLMUL; timed by tools/bench/adversarial/speed.cpp line 172. Simple tabulation: source/fast-polynomials/tools/bench/framework/fast_hashing_arm.h class tabulation_64 (uint64_t table[8][256], XOR of 8 lookups; no SIMD). row.notes: (1) Paper-table key column: the row prints key = L+1 for 'Multiply-shift (fixed length)', but the implementation holds L+1 keys of 128 bits = 2(L+1) 64-bit words (130 words at the 64-word cap), while the caption defines Key as "resident per-key state in 64-bit words"; CLNH's 'L' is consistent (64-bit keys per word), so the multiply-shift entry appears understated by 2x. (2) The 16.5 GB/s comes from adversarial_table/speed_rerun.txt (median 16.48 over 9 runs, min 11.81); the three later passes (speed_pass1-3_arm.jsonl, speed_results.json) give 16.95-16.96, which would print as 17.0. (3) SMHasher3's test failures are not evidence against the bound: multiply-shift is a linear, 2-independent family that by design has no avalanche/BIC behaviour, and the SMHasher3 64-bit implementation additionally departs from the proved scheme (sums only high halves of the products, 256-word key wrap, seed enters as one linear term because the per-seed key regeneration is commented out, keys drawn from Xorshift seeded with 0), which explains the wholesale Seed* failures. (4) SMHasher3 'tabulation' is a composite (multiply-shift block signature, Mersenne-61 polynomial combine, 8x256 simple-tabulation finalizer), not plain tabulation; twisted tabulation is registered nowhere. (5) README bulk figures (1.79, 1.51, 1.89, 2.24, 3.12, 2.20) are marginally below the raw files' 'Average' lines (1.81, 1.52, 1.90, 2.26, 3.14, 2.20); README values reported as instructed, the aggregation difference is in the README generator, not the raw run. (6) Tabulation is absent from tab:injective:adversarial; the only M2 tabulation numbers in the paper are Section 5.7's 1668+-11 us per 10^6 64-bit-integer hashes (3-wise), where the paper's own k=3 hash runs at 886+-13 us. (7) Dietzfelbinger 1996 abstract could not be fetched (Springer cookie wall, Semantic Scholar abstract elided); bibliographic data taken from Thorup's reference [4] and references.bib. ACM DL for the SODA 2013 twisted-tabulation page returned 403; citation taken from Thorup CACM reference [42] ("pages 209–228, 2013"). (8) pdftotext drops overbars and super/subscripts, so quoted formulas read "w ≥ w + ℓ − 1" where the PDF has wbar ≥ w + l − 1, and "[2w ]" for [2^w]; quotes are verbatim to the extracted text on disk. (9) The user (Thomas Dybdahl Ahle) is the original author of the rurban/SMHasher3 multiply_shift and tabulation code (copyright 2020 headers). (10) Twisted-tabulation numbers: no SMHasher entry, no paper measurement; tables 8 KB for 32-bit keys per Thorup CACM Figure 1.

row.family: poly-mersenne-brw-horner: one-key polynomial ("authenticator") hashes — Horner's rule over GF(2^64) and over the Mersenne primes 2^61-1 / 2^89-1, Bernstein's BRW (Bernstein–Rabin–Winograd) polynomial over GF(2^64), and the paper's own injective recurrence instantiated over F_{2^89-1}
row.variants: (a) "Horner, F_2^64" = framework univ_horner_64 (h = h*x + m_i, carryless GF(2^64), 2N-1 multiplications on 2N words, 1 key word); (b) "Horner, unrolled" = framework horner_unrolled_64 (same polynomial, Estrin-style 4-way grouping with x^2,x^4 derived per call); (c) "BRW" = framework univ_brw_64 (Bernstein's H(m_1..m_n) recursive polynomial over GF(2^64), ~n/2 multiplications + lg n squarings per call, 1 key word); (d) "This paper, F_{2^89-1} (89-bit output)" = the paper's injective recurrence P_i = a_i + (b_i+y)(P_{i-1}+x^2) over p = 2^89-1, harness struct PaperMers89Smart (15-byte steps, key 5 words); (e) SMHasher3 poly-mersenne.deg0..deg4 = Horner over 32-bit characters mod p = 2^61-1 with the byte length as first character, followed by a degree-K random-polynomial finalizer (K = 0..4), 32-bit output, credited "Copyright (c) 2020 Thomas Dybdahl Ahle" (the paper's hint names deg1..4); (f) harness-only "Mersenne 2^89-1 Horner" (MersHorner89<8>/<11>, 64-bit key, not a table row).
row.bound_quote: HORNER (Bernstein 2007, Sec. 4.2, pema-20071022.txt lines 409-413): "More generally, for any fixed n, a message m1 , . . . , mn will be protected by the authenticator m1 rn + · · · + mn r + s, where r, s are independent uniform random elements of k. Each forgery attempt has chance at most n/#k of success. The same idea can also be used for any number of messages, as in Sections 2.4 and 2.5, and can be extended to variable-length messages."  BRW (Bernstein 2007, Sec. 5.7, lines 601-609): "More generally, for any fixed n, a message m1 , . . . , mn will be protected by the authenticator rH(m1 , . . . , mn ) + s, where r, s are independent uniform random elements of k. Each forgery attempt has chance at most (2n − 1)/#k of success if n ≥ 1. The same idea can also be used for any number of messages, as in Sections 2.4 and 2.5. Some care is required for variable-length messages. The authenticator can safely be used for messages in S 0 ∪ S 1 ∪ · · · if S ⊂ k satisfies 0 ∈/ S and S ∩ (S + 1) = {}. See Theorem 5.6."  BRW degree/injectivity (Theorem 5.4, lines 509-511): "If n ≤ 2 then deg H(m1 , . . . , mn ) ≤ 1. If n ≥ 3 then H(m1 , . . . , mn ) is a monic polynomial of degree 2blg nc+1 − 1." (Theorem 5.5, lines 527-528): "Then H maps k n injectively to the polynomial ring k[r]."  POLY-MERSENNE (SMHasher3 hashes/poly_mersenne.cpp, code comment; identical in rurban Hashes.cpp lines 1098-1101): "// We first combine hashes using a polynomial in `a`: // hash = x1 + x2 * a + x3 * a^2 + ... (mod p) // This hash has collision probability len/p, since the polynomial is // degree and so can have at most len roots (values of a that make it zero)."  PAPER F_{2^89-1} ROW (sections/injective.tex:33-34): "the family is $n/|\F|$-almost universal on messages of $2n$ field elements: half of Horner's bound at half of Horner's multiplications, with three resident key words. In the single-key specialization $P_n$ has degree $3n+2$ and its three leading coefficients are again the same for every message, so the difference has degree at most $3n-1$ and the family is $(3n-1)/|\F|$-almost universal with one key word." (harness comment, tools/bench/adversarial/speed_hashes.h:232-236: "two keys (x in [0,p), y in [0,2^63)) [...] Total degree N+2 in (x,y); Pr[collision] <= (N+2)*2/2^64."); paper's Horner statement (injective.tex:167): "Horner's $(2n-1)/|\F|$ on the same $2n$ words".
